What should a seller expect from Detroit, Michigan?

Detroit anchors Wayne County as its seat and ranks first in Michigan by population. French explorers founded Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit here in 1701, and by 1920 the auto industry had lifted it to fourth place among American cities. The population then fell from its 1950 peak of 1.85 million, the city filed for bankruptcy in 2013 and left it in 2014, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 649,095 residents sits above the 639,111 counted in 2020.

A seller here deals with 138.7 square miles of land, according to the Census. A house in Boston-Edison or Indian Village competes in a different market from a modest bungalow elsewhere in the city, even though both pay the same city and county taxes. The county records the deed and holds older delinquent tax accounts, so many sale questions end at a county office.

How does the Detroit housing market compare in Census numbers?

Detroit has the lowest home values and the fewest owner-occupants of the four Michigan cities profiled in this batch of pages. Close to half of Detroit households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool.

A typical owned home at $83,900 beside a typical rent of $1,074 means a rented house can repay its price quickly, which is why investors follow Detroit sales. The same gap makes a roof or furnace replacement a much heavier share of a sale price here than in Dearborn, where the typical owned home is $218,800.

What kinds of houses and neighborhoods do Detroit sellers have?

Beyond downtown and New Center, Detroit is mostly low-rise. Working-class areas built before World War II have wood-frame and brick houses, while Brush Park, Woodbridge, Indian Village, Palmer Woods and Boston-Edison have larger, more ornate homes. Forty-two significant structures are on the federal historic register, and the Guardian Building became a National Historic Landmark in 1989.

The ground is flat. The city slopes gently from northwest to southeast over glacial and lake clay, with the Detroit Moraine, a broad clay ridge about 62 feet above the river, under the older districts. Weather and soil shape what an inspector flags:

  • Temperatures stay at or below freezing on roughly 44 days a year, so furnaces, roofs and plumbing get attention.
  • About 12 days a year top 90 degrees, which puts cooling and attic ventilation on the checklist.
  • Clay under older blocks makes basement moisture and drainage fair questions.

Fix these items or price them in before you list.

Which employers, schools and transit options help Detroit buyers?

Midtown's Detroit Medical Center employs more people than anyone else in the city, with Wayne State University beside it and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. General Motors, Rocket Mortgage, Ally Financial and DTE Energy keep headquarters here, and roughly 80,500 people work downtown, one-fifth of the city's jobs. Buyers who work in those districts look for housing nearby.

The river adds a draw of its own. The Detroit River International Wildlife Refuge covers islands, wetlands and shoreline along 48 miles of the Detroit River and western Lake Erie, and the city's attractions bring about 16 million visitors a year. Downtown redevelopment around Campus Martius Park, Grand Circus Park, Ford Field, Comerica Park and Little Caesars Arena adds to the pull.

The Detroit Public Schools district is the largest in Michigan, and charter schools enroll a large additional group. Many families also look at suburban districts, so ask your agent how school boundaries affect the buyer pool on your street.

Getting around is easier than in many Michigan cities. DDOT buses, the QLINE streetcar and the downtown People Mover loop serve the core, and SMART runs routes to the suburbs. Detroit has four crossings to Windsor, Ontario, the newest being the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which opened in 2026.

What state taxes and fees apply when a Detroit house sells?

Michigan puts its deed tax on the seller. Every $500 block of value carries $3.75 of state tax, and a county layer sits on top: 55 cents per block in a county under two million residents. MCL 207.523, 207.525 and 207.504 set the framework, and the Wayne County deed office confirms the current county rate. You have 15 days from handing over the deed to pay the county treasurer.

MCL 207.526 exempts certain deeds, including a court-ordered transfer with no stated price, a foreclosure deed, and an instrument that creates a joint tenancy where one of the owners already held the property. A lender that later resells a foreclosed house does not get the same break.

  • The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a).
  • For the next calendar year, taxable value is set at the SEV.
  • Ask the Detroit assessor for the form that ends your own principal residence exemption.

For current-year and past-due bill amounts, ask the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer for written payoff figures before you sign anything.

Why does tax foreclosure timing matter for Detroit sellers?

The Wayne County Treasurer, whose office is at 400 Monroe Street in Detroit, holds an annual online auction of tax-foreclosed properties. The minimum bid is a fixed amount that includes the treasurer's foreclosure and auction costs, winners have 72 hours to pay in full, and the office records a quit claim deed within 30 days after the auction closes.

Selling before the auction lets you choose the buyer and the price. Ask the treasurer what redemption rights remain on your parcel and whether a payment plan is available. Have the closing agent settle any balance from your proceeds, since a buyer's lender expects the lien cleared when the deed changes hands.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Detroit houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do you compare offers on a Detroit house that needs work?

Three questions decide most Detroit sales: what an appraiser will accept, what an inspector will list, and what taxes are still open on the parcel. A mortgage buyer needs all three to line up. An investor offer skips the appraisal, and an as-is contract can say who clears trash, personal property and open utility accounts.

Line up offers by what you walk away with: price, minus deed tax, minus unpaid taxes and liens, minus repairs you would otherwise fund. Ask each bidder for evidence of funds and a dated closing plan before you choose.

Frequently asked questions

Which side owes the state deed tax on a Detroit house?

The seller. Michigan names the grantor as the liable party. The state takes $3.75 on each $500 block, Wayne County adds its portion, and a court-ordered transfer without a stated price is among the exempt deeds.

Can a Detroit house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes. Request an official payoff letter from the Wayne County Treasurer and let the closing agent settle it out of your proceeds. Selling ahead of the county's foreclosure auction keeps the choice of buyer with you.

How does a sale change the Detroit tax bill?

The buyer's taxable value is reset for the next year to the SEV, the figure the assessor sets at half of market value. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days.

Must I repair my Detroit house before selling?

Buyers and their lenders often ask for repairs, and the contract decides who pays. Ask the City of Detroit about any compliance rules that apply to your property type, especially a rental.

How many people live in Detroit, and what do homes sell for?

Federal estimates for 2025 count 649,095 residents. For 2020 to 2024 the middle price tag on an owned house is $83,900, and about one home in two has its owner living inside.

What sets the pace of a house sale in Grand Rapids?

Pace here follows the neighborhood, the condition of the house and whether a landlord or an owner-occupant holds title. Grand Rapids is the Kent County seat and Michigan's second most populated municipality, with 198,917 residents in 2020 and an estimated 201,183 in 2025. As the economic center of West Michigan, it draws on a metro area of about 1.2 million people.

An owner can hire an agent, sell directly to another party, or accept a cash purchase of the house as it stands. The sections below tie each path to the city's rules, neighborhoods and numbers.

What shapes the Grand Rapids housing market?

Grand Rapids grew along the Grand River, at the rapids that stopped river traffic, and incorporated as a village in 1838 and a city in 1850. It earned the name Furniture City from its furniture makers, and office furniture companies including Steelcase and Haworth are still based in or around the city. Corewell Health is the region's largest employer, with its hospitals and research institutions along the Medical Mile.

The 2024 metro employer list also names Trinity Health, Gordon Food Service, Meijer, Gentex, MillerKnoll, Perrigo, Grand Valley State University and Grand Rapids Public Schools. A deep mix of health care, food, manufacturing and education jobs supports steady housing demand, and the Census Bureau reports that the city's population grew 1.2% from April 2020 to July 2025.

Quality-of-life draws add to the pull. The city hosts the ArtPrize competition, the Grand Rapids Art Museum, the Public Museum and Frederik Meijer Gardens and Sculpture Park, and its craft breweries, Founders among them, earned it the nickname Beer City USA. Gerald R. Ford International Airport serves the region.

  • The Medical Mile brings Corewell Health, the Van Andel Research Institute and Michigan State University's medical school together near downtown.
  • Grand Valley State University's Cook-DeVos Center for Health Sciences and Ferris State's College of Pharmacy sit on the same corridor.
  • Office furniture makers still anchor manufacturing in and around the city.

What do Grand Rapids homes cost, and who lives in them?

Owners and renters split almost evenly, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $244,500.

Grand Rapids statisticResult

Numbers are.

The 19-minute average trip to work is worth mentioning when you describe the house, since the Medical Mile, downtown and the freeways are all close.

Which Grand Rapids neighborhoods and roads do buyers ask about?

The city lists 37 distinct neighborhoods, among them Heritage Hill, Eastown, East Hills, Alger Heights, Creston, Garfield Park, Midtown, Belknap Lookout, Roosevelt Park and the North End. Mailing addresses are divided into NE, NW, SE and SW quadrants, with Fulton Street as the north-south dividing line and Division Avenue as the east-west one, so check the quadrant in any address you quote.

Highways shape commute choices. I-96 runs along the north and northeast sides, I-196 crosses east to west, US 131 runs north to south, and M-6 loops the south side. The Rapid operates the buses, including the SilverLine bus rapid transit route that opened in 2014, and DASH shuttles are free downtown.

How does Grand Rapids regulate rental houses before a sale?

The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit. Owners register rental properties every year, and registration is free. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant. Certificates run two, four or six years depending on the property, and the city sends a reminder 90 days before recertification.

A rental inspection can end three ways. With no violations, the owner receives a certificate. With minor violations, the inspector gives verbal orders with a 14-day repair deadline. With major violations, a Notice of Violation sets a deadline of 60 or 120 days. Tenants should get 48 hours of notice before an inspection. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

  • A landlord with a certified rental can hand the buyer a clean compliance record.
  • A rental that is vacant needs a vacant-property registration.
  • Rentals that use fuel-burning equipment must pass a mechanical safety inspection as part of certification.

Do Grand Rapids short-term rental and accessory unit rules matter?

They can if the property has a second unit. The city's zoning ordinance allows accessory dwelling units on single and two-family lots, and a June 2026 update allows an accessory unit of up to 1,000 square feet that is never larger than the main house. An accessory unit cannot be rented for fewer than 30 days, so Airbnb and Vrbo style use is not allowed, and a leased unit must be registered and certified as a rental. A deed restriction must be recorded so the unit is not conveyed separately from the house.

If your property has a second unit or a rented room, ask the Planning Department at planning@grcity.us before you list so the paperwork matches what you advertise.

How does Grand Rapids weather affect a house for sale?

Lake Michigan lies about 25 miles west, and the city averages 75.6 inches of snow a year, among the highest totals of any major American city. Lake-effect storms can arrive suddenly. Winters are cold and cloudy, summers are warm and humid, and the average growing season runs about 162 days, from a last spring frost near May 1 to a first fall frost near October 11.

Roofs, gutters, furnaces and basement moisture draw close attention from buyers in that climate. A seller who lists in winter should have the furnace serviced and the roof checked first.

What does the Michigan transfer tax cost on a Grand Rapids sale?

Michigan's county tax of 55 cents and state tax of $3.75 on each $500 of price are the seller's to pay (MCL 207.504 and 207.525), and the Kent County treasurer collects within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523).

At the city's median value of $244,500 that totals roughly $2,100, and the settlement statement will show the exact figure. The buyer notifies the assessor within 45 days so taxable value can reset to the state equalized value the next calendar year (MCL 211.27a), and a higher bill for the buyer is a common talking point in negotiation.

When does an as-is sale beat a listing in Grand Rapids?

Strong buyer demand favors a traditional listing for a house in good repair. An as-is sale fits deferred maintenance, an estate, tenant trouble or a firm moving date.

  • A listing fits an updated house when you can allow time for showings and financing.
  • An as-is buyer fits a vacant house, one with open code orders, or one that needs work before a lender would approve a loan.
  • Another landlord may pay a premium for a property that already holds a current Certificate of Compliance.

Ask for proof of funds, weigh offers by net proceeds, and put the closing date in writing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does a rented Grand Rapids house need a compliance certificate?

Yes. The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit, so a rented house should hold a current one. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

Must I register an empty house in Grand Rapids?

Yes. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant, and registration is free. You can register online, by mail or at the Code Compliance office on Monroe Avenue NW.

Is an accessory unit allowed as a short-term rental?

No. The city bars accessory units from rentals under 30 days, and a leased unit must be registered and certified through Code Compliance.

What would Michigan transfer tax come to on a $244,500 Grand Rapids sale?

Roughly $2,100, from 55 cents per $500 for the county plus $3.75 per $500 for the state. The seller owes it, and the settlement statement lists the exact amount.

Will a Grand Rapids buyer pay more in property tax than I do?

Usually. Taxable value resets to the state equalized value in the calendar year after the transfer, and the buyer must notify the assessor within 45 days.

What should a Warren homeowner know before selling a house?

Three local pieces shape a Warren sale: a few Building Division and rental rules, the Macomb County recording office in Mount Clemens, and a tax calendar that splits between city and county. Warren is Macomb County's biggest community and the state's third-largest city, so title agents and inspectors here run through these items all the time.

Accepting a cash offer on an as-is basis skips the showings and the repair list. It does nothing to the recording step, the seller's transfer tax, or any city bill still attached to the parcel. The headings below follow the order in which a seller usually runs into each one.

What is Warren like as a place to own a house?

Warren occupies a six-by-six mile square at the southwest tip of Macomb County, between 8 Mile Road and 14 Mile Road, and it wraps around the small city of Center Line. The city is 34.4 square miles, and its entire southern edge touches Detroit. Beebe's Corners, the first settlement, began in 1830 at Mound Road and Chicago Road. Voters made Warren a city on January 1, 1957.

Growth came fast: 42,653 people in 1950, then 179,260 by 1970, fed by the Detroit Arsenal Tank Plant, a Chrysler truck plant and the General Motors Technical Center. Southeast Warren has many bungalows from the years right after World War II. North of Stephens Road, a lot of the housing is brick ranches from after 1960.

  • Southeast Warren takes in Warrendale, Belangers Garden, Berkshire Manor and Piper Van Dyke.
  • Southwest Warren holds Fitzgerald and Beierman Farms.
  • Northeast Warren includes Bear Creek, Bella Vista Estates, Fairlane Estates and downtown.
  • Northwest Warren is mostly the west half of Warren Con.

Cold matters for a house of this age. NOAA normals show about 39 days a year when Warren never climbs above freezing, so a buyer's inspector will look hard at the furnace, roof and pipes.

Who employs Warren residents, and how do the roads connect them?

According to the city's 2022 financial report, General Motors employs 23,823 people in Warren. The federal government is next at 7,800, tied to the Detroit Arsenal. Stellantis has 5,523, Ascension Health 2,407 and Lipari Foods 1,300. Steady payrolls like these keep a pool of local buyers in the market.

I-696 runs east and west across the city. Van Dyke Avenue (M-53) divides it north from south, Groesbeck Highway (M-97) angles through the southeast corner, and Mound Road is a second major north-south route. SMART runs the buses. Warren workers spend a mean of 24.9 minutes getting to work, per the Census Bureau.

Macomb Intermediate School District oversees the six public districts that serve Warren, and Macomb Community College keeps a campus here. District lines wind through neighborhoods, so check the district tied to a particular address instead of trusting a street name.

What do the Census figures say about Warren housing?

Warren's estimated population for July 1, 2025 is 137,138, which sits 1.6 percent below the April 2020 base. From 2020 through 2024 the Census counted 54,744 households of roughly 2.5 people, and 71.1 percent of them owned their home.

Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $193,400. Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,225, and the median household income is $64,016. Typical monthly owner costs are $1,403 for those with a mortgage and $557 for those without. A single block can look quite different from any of these citywide numbers.

Which Warren city rules affect a sale?

Warren's residential city certification, as the posted application describes it, covers a vacant dwelling that has been posted "no occupancy": nobody may move in until the Building Division confirms the house meets the International Property Maintenance Code and the zoning ordinance. The office is at One City Square, Suite 305 (586-574-4504).

Rental owners face more. The rental ordinance posted by the Rental Inspections Division sets these terms:

  • No one may rent or occupy a rental dwelling without a rental license, and licenses do not transfer between landlords or units.
  • A license lasts two years and needs a biennial inspection.
  • Sale of the property ends the license immediately.
  • No license is issued until prior property taxes, special assessments, water or sewer bills and mowing or cleanup charges are paid.

If tenants live in the house, call the Rental Inspections Division at 586-574-4633 and find out where the license stands before you list. Open balances there are easy to miss.

The same Building Division enforces the Michigan Building Code and Michigan Residential Code, which every Michigan community has had to adopt since 2004, along with Warren's zoning ordinance. A sunroom, deck or finished basement built without a permit is the kind of item that surfaces during a buyer's walkthrough, so gather permit records for past work early.

Where does a Warren deed get recorded, and what are the charges?

Warren lies in Macomb County, so the deed is filed with the county Register of Deeds at 120 N. Main St. in Mount Clemens (phone 586-469-7953). Counter hours run weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:15 p.m. A flat per-document fee has applied since October 1, 2016, whatever the page count.

Macomb County recording charges. Source: Macomb County Register of Deeds recording fee and transfer tax pages.
ItemCharge
Deed, mortgage or other instrument$30 per document
Document assigning or discharging several instruments$3 added for each extra instrument
Tax certificate (warranty deeds, land contracts)$5 for up to five legal descriptions
State transfer taxSale price multiplied by .0075
Macomb County transfer taxSale price multiplied by .0011

Before a warranty deed or land contract is accepted, it needs a tax certificate from the county treasurer. The seller carries the transfer tax. Macomb publishes a schedule in $500 steps for anyone who wants the exact figure for a price.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Warren houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When are Warren property taxes due?

The City of Warren sends summer bills (city and school) in early July and winter bills (county) in early December. The dates below come from the Treasurer's tax payment page; the Treasurer's Office at 586-574-4542 can confirm them for the current year.

  • Pay the summer bill whole, or split it by paying the first half by August 31. The second half is billed December 1 and due January 31.
  • From September 1 only the entire summer balance is taken, with a 1 percent fee that month and half a percent for every month after.
  • The winter bill is payable December 1 through February 28.
  • A balance still open after February 28 goes to the Macomb County Treasurer, with a further 4 percent fee and 1 percent interest monthly.

Ask your title agent how these will be divided at closing. An unpaid bill can hold up a rental license or a clear title, so call the Treasurer's Office before you accept an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a city inspection to sell my Warren house?

The city certification on Warren's posted application covers vacant houses marked no occupancy, which must pass a Building Division inspection before anyone moves in. Phone 586-574-4504 to learn whether your parcel carries that posting.

What happens to a Warren rental license when the property sells?

It ends at once. The rental ordinance says a sale terminates the license and that licenses cannot move between owners. The new owner applies again and the unit is inspected afresh.

Who pays transfer tax when a Warren house sells?

The seller does. Macomb County prints the state rate as .0075 times the sale price and the county rate as .0011 times the sale price, and both are collected at recording.

Which office records the deed on a Warren sale?

The Macomb County Register of Deeds in Mount Clemens. The fee is $30 for the document, and a warranty deed first needs a tax certificate from the county treasurer.

What if I am behind on Warren property taxes before a sale?

Pay the Warren Treasurer's Office before the winter bill's February 28 cutoff. After that the balance moves to the Macomb County Treasurer with added fees and monthly interest, so clear it or have the title agent include it in the payoff.

Which selling routes move fastest in Sterling Heights?

Owners here have three working routes. A broker can market the house, you can look for a buyer yourself, or an investor can buy it for cash. Brokered sales tend to pay the most, and investor purchases tend to close soonest.

A mortgage buyer adds steps. The lender orders an appraisal, an inspector writes a report, and either document can reopen a price you thought was settled. A cash buyer skips those steps, which appeals to owners of worn-out roofs and dated kitchens in the older subdivisions.

  • Brokered sale: biggest pool of buyers, a commission at closing, and weeks or months to the right offer.
  • Private sale: no commission, but contract, showings and deed are yours to arrange.
  • Cash purchase: the buyer accepts the property as is, and the closing date is part of the deal.

Have each bidder write price, closing date, tax responsibility and inspection rights on one page, then compare what reaches you after payoff and costs.

Where is Sterling Heights, and how did it grow?

The city occupies about 36 square miles of Macomb County, a second-ring suburb well north of the Detroit core. Warren is its southern neighbor, Troy sits across the western line, Utica and Shelby Township lie north, and Clinton Township lies east.

Surveyors mapped the land in 1818, and Sterling Township took its name in 1838. Farms, with rhubarb as a notable crop shipped to Detroit, covered it until the 1950s. Better roads and the boom in auto-industry jobs then filled it with subdivisions, and Chrysler and Ford plant workers made up much of the 1960s and 1970s population. Residents voted to incorporate in 1968. The suffix Heights came from a state rule against two incorporated places sharing a name, since a tiny village called Sterling already existed in Arenac County. Lakeside Mall followed in 1976.

Later arrivals included many Albanian, Bosnian, Polish and Serbian families, and after 2003 a large Assyrian and Chaldean Catholic community that gave the area near 15 Mile and Ryan roads the nickname Little Nineveh. The Clinton River crosses the northeast corner on the way to Lake St. Clair. Days that never climb above freezing number about 39 a year, which is why buyers ask about furnaces and roofs.

How much do homes cost and who lives in them?

Census data for 2020 through 2024 show 51,736 households and a typical home value of $274,300 among owners. Most of the housing is owner-occupied, so the people touring your house are mostly future residents.

Over a third of residents (35.2%) use another language at home, so clear photos and plain written terms help a sale.

Which schools and roads matter to buyers?

Utica Community Schools covers the northern half of Sterling Heights, and Warren Consolidated Schools covers the southern half. Utica operates Stevenson High School and Henry Ford II High School here, while Warren Consolidated runs Sterling Heights High School. Parkway Christian School serves private-school families from kindergarten through twelfth grade.

The line runs through the middle of town, so similar houses a mile apart can feed different high schools. Name the district in your listing.

  • M-53 (Van Dyke) heads north toward the Thumb and south toward Detroit.
  • M-59 (Hall Road) links Macomb and Oakland counties and lines up the shopping district around Lakeside Mall.
  • Mound Road is the long north-south artery, and the numbered mile roads from 14 through 20 handle east-west trips. Sixteen Mile doubles as Metro Parkway.

Houses along these corridors sell on convenience. Streets farther in sell on lot size and schools.

What transfer tax applies to a Sterling Heights sale?

The seller is liable, and the county treasurer expects payment within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523). The state tax runs $3.75 for each $500 of value, rounded up (MCL 207.525).

On the county's published schedule, the price is multiplied by .0075 for the state share and .0011 for the county share. The title agent's settlement statement shows the real total.

Some deeds are exempt under MCL 207.526, among them gifts to children and grandchildren and deeds in foreclosure. An exempt deed must quote the statute and lettered subsection.

How does a sale change the buyer's tax bill?

The buyer's bill can come out well above yours. After a transfer, Taxable Value steps up to State Equalized Value, and the yearly cap on increases begins again from that level.

Per the city, a Property Transfer Affidavit (Form 2766) is the buyer's job, due at Assessing in 45 days. A seller who claimed a Principal Residence Exemption files Form 2602 to end it. Owners who bought first and sell second can ask to keep the old exemption up to three years, provided the vacated house stays listed, unrented and free of business use.

  • Summer bill: arrives in late June, payable from July 1 into early September.
  • Winter bill: arrives in late November, payable from December 1 through February.
  • A summer balance left after Labor Day grows monthly, and an added 3% lands on March 1 as the account moves to the county.

Notices of assessment are mailed at the end of February, and a March Board of Review hears appeals. Reach Assessing at 586-446-2340 and the treasury at 586-446-2780.

The city treasury sits at 40555 Utica Road and is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and it keeps drop boxes on the city center campus for payments. Once a bill passes March 1, payment moves to the Macomb County Building at 1 South Main in Mount Clemens, phone 586-469-5190. Escrow agents receive the original bills, so a seller with an escrow account should confirm that the final bill was paid before the closing date.

How is the deed recorded in Macomb County?

Recording takes place at the county Register of Deeds, 120 N. Main St., Mount Clemens, (586) 469-7953. Title agents usually deliver the deed, but private sellers should know what gets paper rejected.

  • Ink signatures in the original, each name printed below, and a notary block spelling every name identically.
  • Buyer addresses and the preparer's details on the deed itself.
  • A tall top margin on page one (2.5 inches) and narrow ones (half an inch) elsewhere.
  • A recorded, referenced death certificate if an owner has died.

A rejected deed pushes back the buyer's title, and your payout with it.

How should you compare competing offers?

Rank offers by net proceeds, speed and the odds of closing. A slightly higher bid with a long inspection window can lose to a modest cash bid with a fixed date.

Confirm who buys the title policy, whether leftover belongings stay, and whether the buyer may assign the contract to someone else. With a mortgage, get a written payoff letter first, since that balance comes off your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Sterling Heights house in poor shape still sell?

Yes. Some buyers will contract for it as is, and cash buyers do so most often. Financed buyers may ask for repairs once the appraisal arrives.

Who covers the transfer tax at a Sterling Heights closing?

The statute makes the seller liable, though your contract can say otherwise. Your settlement statement lists the state and Macomb County amounts.

Will taxes jump for whoever buys my house?

They can. The year after a transfer, Taxable Value resets to State Equalized Value. The buyer reports the purchase on the Property Transfer Affidavit.

Where does the Sterling Heights deed go after closing?

It is recorded with the Macomb County Register of Deeds. The office will return it if signatures, margins or notary details are off.

Which district will the buyer's children attend?

Utica Community Schools covers the north half of the city and Warren Consolidated Schools the south half. The street address decides.

How did Ann Arbor's history shape its housing stock?

In 1956 voters merged the city of East Ann Arbor into Ann Arbor, and the current City Hall opened in 1963 after a 1960 bond vote. The 1960s and 1970s brought a reputation for student activism, including the first U.S. teach-in against the Vietnam War in 1965, and the Human Rights Party won council seats on the student vote in the early 1970s.

Ann Arbor began as a land speculators' plat registered with Wayne County in 1824 and grew around two anchors: the county seat, awarded in 1827, and the University of Michigan, which took over land first offered to the state as a capitol site. The city lost that capitol bid to Lansing, accepted the university in 1837, and incorporated as a city in 1851.

Long before that, Anishinaabe peoples lived and traveled through the area, and the land was ceded to the United States under the 1807 Treaty of Detroit. The Huron River gives the city its hilly shape. Elevation runs from about 750 feet along the water to 1,015 feet on the west side, which is why houses on the slopes have different drainage, views and basements than those on flat ground.

The Tree Town nickname rests on 50,000 trees along streets and as many again in parks. Emerald ash borers have killed many of the city's roughly 10,500 ash trees, a fact worth knowing if a mature ash stands near your house or the sewer line.

Why is the Ann Arbor housing market unlike most of Michigan?

Renters, graduate students and short stays drive much of the market, and prices sit far above state norms. Owning a typical home costs $2,436 a month with a mortgage, compared with a $1,649 median rent.

Ann Arbor in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 survey

About one resident in three had a different address a year earlier, and 18.6 percent were born abroad. Because owners live in fewer than half of homes, many houses are rentals, and prospective buyers will raise licensing early.

What does the University of Michigan mean for an Ann Arbor seller?

It means a deep, stable pool of employed buyers and renters. The university employs about 30,000 people, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center, and research money brings in technology firms, labs and startups.

The technology history goes back to the 1930s, when the Kadette radio was made here. Today the list includes Duo Security, a KLA North American headquarters that opened in 2021, a regional Google office, Internet2 and Merit Network, and more than twenty video game and XR studios. Federal sites add to the base, among them a NOAA Great Lakes laboratory and an EPA vehicle emissions laboratory. Auto firms such as General Motors and Visteon also employ residents.

Census figures show 77.9 percent of adults with a bachelor's degree and a 20.0 minute average commute, and about 36 percent of 2019 trips were on foot, by bike or on transit.

Which roads, parks and schools matter when you list an Ann Arbor house?

Buyers check three things: how a house connects to the freeways, whether it sits near parks, and which high school it feeds.

  • US-23 hugs the east side, M-14 the north and I-94 the south and west, while Michigan Avenue, Washtenaw Avenue and Ford Road carry cross-town traffic.
  • TheRide runs buses across the city and into Ypsilanti, and Amtrak's Wolverine stops at the Ann Arbor station.
  • More than 160 parks include Buhr Park, Fuller Recreation Area and a 30,000 square foot skatepark that opened in 2014 inside Veterans Memorial Park.
  • Ann Arbor Public Schools had 17,070 students in 2021 to 2022 and runs Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community high schools, with a well-known music program.

Private and charter choices include Greenhills School, Clonlara School and Michigan Islamic Academy. The Border-to-Border Trail links the city with Ypsilanti along the river for walkers and cyclists, and photos of it sell houses nearby.

What does Ann Arbor's weather mean for a house?

Winters are cold and snowy, with January highs near 32 degrees and snowfall of about 61 inches a season, normally from November to April. Summers are warm and humid, with July highs around 84 degrees and 10 days at or above 90. Precipitation totals about 38 inches a year, heaviest in summer.

Those numbers matter to a buyer's inspector. Roofs, gutters, basement walls and sump pumps carry the load in a place with this much snow and rain, so gather receipts for roof and drainage work before you list. Ask any serious buyer whether they plan an inspection, and offer your repair records up front.

Can a buyer run a short-term rental in an Ann Arbor house?

Only with a city license, and the zoning rules narrow who can get one. Chapter 97 of the city code covers stays of 30 consecutive days or fewer, and the license costs $500 per unit each year.

  • In zones whose names begin with R, only the owner's principal residence can qualify, backed by a sworn statement of principal residency.
  • Accessory dwelling units cannot be short-term rentals.
  • Companies acting for an owner cannot hold a license, and neither can a tenant who never moved in.
  • A non-owner-occupied property in a zone that permits one needs a valid Certificate of Compliance first.
  • Apply and pay through the city's STREAM portal. Review takes up to 21 business days, denied applications are not refunded, and the license renews yearly.

Some investors picture a vacation rental and then learn the zone forbids it. For long-term renting, the city runs a Green Rental Housing program with a HERS energy score of 110 or lower as its pass mark.

How do Ann Arbor assessments, appeals and transfers work?

The Assessor's Office on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St., takes the transfer affidavit and the exemption forms in person, by mail or through the city's online submission page, and answers at 734.794.6530. New owners file the Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, and sellers rescind their own principal residence exemption on the old home.

Property tax supplies more than half of city revenue. Taxable value moves each year by the inflation multiplier or 5 percent, whichever is lower, and a sale lifts it back toward assessed value. Notices go out in early March, and the Board of Review sits for four days beginning the Monday of the third week of March. A residential owner who is turned down there has until July 31 to go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

What does recording a deed cost for an Ann Arbor property?

Washtenaw County has fewer than 2,000,000 residents, so the county tax is 55 cents per $500 and the state tax is $3.75 per $500. A $450,000 house owes $3,870 at recording, and the seller pays. State law sets the recording fee at $30 per document, but a charter county may set its own, so ask the Washtenaw County Register of Deeds for its table.

Warranty deeds need a county treasurer tax certificate. Exemptions cover transfers under $100, gifts from parent to child or grandparent to grandchild, and court-ordered transfers that set no price.

Frequently asked questions

Do owners or renters hold most Ann Arbor homes?

Renters hold the larger share. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 45.5 percent for 2020 to 2024.

How long does the short-term rental review take in Ann Arbor?

Up to 21 business days after the $500 payment. Applications go through the city's STREAM portal.

What is the combined transfer tax on a $450,000 Ann Arbor sale?

It is $3,870, from $8.60 per $1,000. The seller pays it when the deed is recorded.

Where do I file sale paperwork with the Ann Arbor assessor?

Larcom City Hall, fifth floor, 301 E. Huron St., or online. The office is reachable at 734.794.6530.

How snowy are Ann Arbor winters?

Snowfall averages about 61 inches a season, falling mostly from November to April, and January highs sit near 32 degrees.

What is different about selling a house in Lansing?

As Michigan's capital, Lansing straddles three counties. Most parcels are in Ingham, some are in Eaton to the west, and some in Clinton to the north, which decides where your deed is recorded. Look at your tax bill first.

The July 2025 estimate is 113,884 residents, 1.1 percent more than the 2020 base. Homes here are valued well under Kentwood's or Livonia's, and only a little over half are owner-occupied, so a good share of sellers are landlords.

Lansing is also the center of a metro area of roughly 473,000 people, the third largest in Michigan. Michigan State University sits in neighboring East Lansing rather than in the city, and the Census counts 39.14 square miles of land inside Lansing itself. Some of that land, such as the airport tract, came under city control through temporary Michigan land-sharing agreements known as 425 agreements, which are not annexations under state law.

How did Lansing get its shape, and which neighborhoods matter to a seller?

Lansing was chosen as the capital in 1847 because it was more central and safer than Detroit, and it was incorporated as a city in 1859. Ransom Olds built Oldsmobile and later REO Motor Car here, and REO Town along Washington Avenue grew up around his factories.

The city is usually described in four sections, and buyers use the same names:

  • Eastside, east of the Grand River, centered on Michigan Avenue and the Frandor shopping center
  • Westside, around the river's curve, the most mixed by income and home type
  • Northwestside, the smallest section, near the Capital Region International Airport
  • Southside, the fourth section

Old Town, with buildings from the mid-1800s, and REO Town, along Washington Avenue, are the two historic districts people mention first. A listing that names its section and nearest corridor is easier for buyers to place.

Who buys houses in Lansing, and what keeps demand steady?

Government, education, insurance and health care keep Lansing's job base broad. A 2018 ranking by the Lansing Economic Area Partnership put the State of Michigan first with about 14,400 jobs, followed by Michigan State University, University of Michigan Health-Sparrow, General Motors, Lansing Community College, McLaren Greater Lansing and Auto-Owners Insurance. Jackson National Life and Delta Dental also appear on that list.

State and university payrolls mean steady renters and first-time buyers, and investors also look for small, older houses. If your house is a rental, expect investor interest first. If it is owner-occupied and updated, the broader market may pay more.

The school picture is mixed. Lansing School District covers most of the city, yet pieces fall into Holt, East Lansing, Okemos, Mason, Waverly, Grand Ledge and DeWitt, so confirm the district by address.

How easy is it to get around Lansing, and does that help a listing?

Lansing is crossed by I-96, I-69, I-496, US-127, M-43 along Saginaw Street and Grand River Avenue, and M-99 on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. Drivers reach Detroit or Grand Rapids in one highway run, which matters to buyers who commute or work for the state.

The Capital Area Transportation Authority runs 33 bus routes, and the Capital Region International Airport has scheduled flights and a UPS freight hub. A house within walking distance of a bus line or the river trail is worth naming in the listing text.

Winters are cold and summers warm and humid. Snow arrives between early November and early April and averages 51.1 inches a season, and the temperature falls to 0 degrees Fahrenheit or lower on about ten nights a year. The city is largely spared the lake-effect snow that hits Grand Rapids.

For an older Lansing house, those numbers point to the usual trouble spots: aging boilers and furnaces, thin attic insulation, frost-damaged porches and wet basements. Do Lansing landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes. Lansing requires every rental property to be registered with Code Compliance, with the exception of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling. The fee schedule effective July 1, 2024 lists a $235 new registration fee, a $55 per building fee for a change of owner, and a base inspection fee of $175 per building for one and two family structures.

When a rental is sold, the buyer takes on the registration, the inspection history and any open citations. Late fees and failure-to-register fees are listed on the same schedule, so an unregistered rental costs more to sell than a registered one. Ask Code Compliance for the current forms before you list a rental.

Vacant houses face a separate risk. The schedule includes administrative fees for red-tagged properties, emergency board-up and demolition, all of which can be assessed against the parcel.

The March hearing dates and the other 2026 entries are now in the past, but they fall in the same weeks every year. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when unpaid bills move to the county, because that date decides who you pay at closing.

What happens at closing and after a sale in Lansing?

Your deed goes to whichever of the three county recorders holds the parcel. The state tax on it is $3.75 per $500 of price, a county tax is added on top, and a handful of family transfers escape both. The title company can tell you which line applies.

Within 45 days of closing the buyer reports the sale to Lansing's assessor, and the house's taxable value is rebased for the following year. You, meanwhile, have 90 days after moving out to cancel your homestead school-tax exemption.

What should a Dearborn homeowner know before selling?

Dearborn is a first-ring suburb in Wayne County that touches Detroit on the north and east, about seven miles west of downtown Detroit. The city covers roughly 24.5 square miles and grew up on both banks of the Rouge River. The neighboring village of Fordson, once called Springwells, merged with Dearborn in a 1928 vote.

The Ford Motor Company world headquarters, the Ford River Rouge complex and The Henry Ford museum campus shape the local housing market. Many owners here live close to a Ford job, a hospital or one of the two colleges, and buyers often start their search with commute time.

How does the Dearborn pre-sale inspection work?

The seller, the listing agent or a legally appointed power of attorney files a residential inspection request with the city's Economic Development Department and pays the fee with it. City staff then call to set the visit, which takes about 45 minutes. An adult aged 18 or older must be home for the whole inspection.

The inspector checks basic safety and property maintenance against the city's minimum housing standards, then issues a written report. Every item on that report counts as a code violation and has to be fixed and re-inspected. The sequence runs like this:

  • Submit the application and payment.
  • Wait for staff to schedule the inspection.
  • Be present for the walk-through and keep the report.
  • Correct each listed item; the clock is twelve months from the first inspection day.
  • Request a re-inspection and pass it.
  • Email the buyer's name to the city sales address and say whether the buyer is the occupant, so the certificate can be prepared.

A report holds for twelve months, so a house that falls out of contract can be relisted without a second full inspection while that window is open.

Dearborn Public Schools operates 34 schools and serves more than 18,000 students, making it the fourth-largest district in Michigan. The main high schools are Fordson High School, Dearborn High School and Edsel Ford High School. Private and charter options include Divine Child, Henry Ford Academy inside Greenfield Village, and Advanced Technology Academy.

The University of Michigan-Dearborn and Henry Ford College sit next to each other on Evergreen Road. Ford dwarfs every other employer in the 2022 annual report the city files, followed by Beaumont Health and the school district. Carhartt, AAA Michigan and Cleveland-Cliffs Dearborn Works also appear among the top ten.

Buyers who commute tend to ask about travel time, and the Census lists a mean of 21.7 minutes for Dearborn workers. Fairlane Town Center, the Henry Ford Centennial Library and the Fair Lane estate give the city's middle section a lot of green and civic space, much of it kept open on land Henry Ford once assembled.

How do Dearborn property taxes work for a seller?

Dearborn sends two bills a year, and each carries different taxing bodies. Whichever bill is open at your closing decides what the settlement statement shows.

  • The summer bill is levied July 1 and due September 14. It holds the school tax, the city tax and the county-allocated operating tax, and an owner can pay it in three pieces (September 14, November 14, January 14) for a one-time $3 charge.
  • The winter bill is levied December 1 and due February 14. The county's remaining levies and the city's combined sewer overflow debt ride on it, and the whole amount is paid at once.
  • Before closing, ask the Treasury Division for a written payoff so the closing agent sends the right amount.

The cashier counter is at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, on weekdays, closing at half past four. The Assessment Department shares the building and answers value questions at 313-943-2140.

What costs and filings come with a Dearborn sale?

Michigan puts the transfer tax on the seller. On every $500 block of sale value the state takes $3.75 (MCL 207.525), and Wayne County adds its own levy under MCL 207.504, which sets 55 cents per block in counties under two million residents. Ask Wayne County's deed office for that figure before you build a net sheet.

MCL 207.526 carves out some deeds. Dearborn owners most often meet the exemption for a deed between spouses that changes how they hold title, and the one for a land contract whose legal title has not yet passed.

After closing, the buyer notifies the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a). The city's assessment guide describes the next step: for the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. If you held a principal residence exemption, ask the Dearborn assessor for the form that removes it.

Which selling route fits a Dearborn house with open inspection items?

A listed sale usually brings the highest price but makes you finish every cited repair before closing. An investor who plans to renovate or rent the house faces the same certificate requirement, and the city asks whether the buyer intends to live there. A private sale lets you and the buyer agree in writing on who pays for corrections, which helps when the inspection list is long.

A long list is the usual reason a Dearborn sale slips. Book the inspection early, settle in writing who handles each correction, and keep the report in your closing file.

Is a city inspection required before my Dearborn house can close?

Yes. Dearborn will not let a sale close without a Certificate of Occupancy, and the certificate follows a pre-sale inspection. You, your agent or a power of attorney requests the visit, fixes any violations, passes a re-inspection and then emails the buyer's name to city staff so the certificate is issued in that name.

How long is a Dearborn inspection report valid?

Twelve months, counting from the first inspection. That is also your window to correct every listed violation and pass the re-inspection, so a failed sale does not force a second full inspection if you relist inside it.

When are Dearborn property taxes due?

Summer taxes are due September 14 and winter taxes February 14. The summer bill may be split into payments on September 14, November 14 and January 14. The winter bill has no split option.

Who pays the state transfer tax in a Dearborn sale?

The seller. Michigan makes the grantor liable, at $3.75 for each $500 block of value for the state plus the Wayne County levy. A few deeds are exempt, such as a spouse's deed creating a tenancy by the entireties.

How does a Dearborn sale change the tax bill?

It usually rises for the buyer. For the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. Your own exemption ends once you rescind it with the assessor.

What makes selling a house in Livonia different from other Michigan cities?

Livonia is a big western suburb, roughly 20 miles northwest of downtown Detroit, where 87.2 percent of housing is owner-occupied. That ratio means most sales are ordinary owner-to-buyer transfers, with a smaller group of rentals that fall under a strict city licensing program.

The Census Bureau estimates 92,603 residents for July 1, 2025, a 3.1 percent drop from the 2020 base of 95,529. In the 2020 count the median age was 45.6, and residents 65 and over made up 21.5 percent.

How did Livonia grow into the city it is now?

Livonia Township was organized in 1835 and named for Livonia, New York, where many early settlers came from. Residents voted to become a city on May 23, 1950, partly to collect tax revenue from the Detroit Race Course, which closed in 1998 and was redeveloped.

Census counts went from 17,634 in 1950 to 66,702 in 1960 and 110,109 in 1970, so a great deal of the housing was built in those postwar years. The city covers about 35.7 square miles of land, with Newburgh Lake and Nankin Lake in the south and southwest linked by Hines Drive.

Gather your permit history before you list. The city issues the permits for additions, decks, basement finishing and similar work, and open permits or violations are tracked by the Inspection Department.

Livonia's largest employers include Ford Motor Company, Trinity Health, Livonia Public Schools, St. Mary Mercy Hospital, Schoolcraft College, ZF Automotive and United Parcel Service. Laurel Park Place, a mall opened in 1989 at Six Mile and Newburgh roads, anchors retail, and former mall sites were redeveloped as Wonderland Village and Livonia Marketplace.

Most addresses fall in Livonia Public Schools, which runs Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. A portion of northeast Livonia is served by the Clarenceville School District. Franklin offers the International Baccalaureate program for select students, Churchill houses a math, science and computer program plus a creative and performing arts program, and Stevenson has a global education school. Madonna University and Schoolcraft College are also in the city.

The district runs two early childhood centers, thirteen elementary schools, four upper elementary schools, three middle schools and three high schools. Frost Middle School hosts the MACAT program for academically talented students, and Webster Elementary hosts a similar program for younger grades.

Confirm which district serves your address before you describe the school zone in a listing.

The guide also applies the state occupancy standard of 225 square feet for the first person and 70 for each additional person, not counting baths or closets. Common rental violations in the guide include dryer venting, missing smoke alarms and GFCI outlets, and a furnace carbon monoxide check every three years by a licensed mechanical contractor. When are Livonia property taxes due, and who is paid?

Livonia bills real and personal property taxes on July 1 and December 1. The summer bill's deadline is September 14. The Treasurer then splits the collections among the money to the city, two school districts (Livonia and Clarenceville), Schoolcraft College, the state education tax, Wayne County, Wayne RESA and the Oakland ISD.

Delinquent real property taxes go to the Wayne County Treasurer. For outstanding permits, violations, vacant or abandoned registration fees or Certificate of Occupancy questions, the Treasurer's page tells you to call the Inspection Department, because those fees do not show on the online tax inquiry. Special assessment requests go by email to the Treasurer's office.

Check the city's online property inquiry before closing so your title company can see the tax history for the parcel.

How is a Livonia deed recorded and taxed?

Livonia sits inside Wayne County, so the Wayne County Register of Deeds handles recording. A deed first needs the county treasurer's tax certification unless an exemption applies. The register's schedule from January 1, 2026 lists $26 per document plus a $4 survey fee where applicable, and service is by appointment.

Michigan's state transfer tax works out to $3.75 per $500 of sale price, and the Wayne County levy is separate, so the title company should quote both. Gifts to children and grandchildren are among the listed exemptions.

Closing starts two clocks. The buyer has 45 days to report the transfer to Livonia's assessor, and you have 90 days from moving out to cancel a homestead exemption you no longer qualify for.

The county register of deeds, after the county treasurer certifies the taxes. Service there is by appointment.

Billing goes out July 1 for summer, with a September 14 deadline that rolls to the next business day on weekends and holidays. Winter bills follow on December 1.

Send the Inspection Department the purchase agreement so a scheduled inspection can be cancelled or kept to clear violations. The city inspects rentals at a change of ownership, so call 734-466-2580.

Most of the city is in Livonia Public Schools, which runs Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. A portion of northeast Livonia is in the Clarenceville School District, so check the district for your address.

Where is Troy, and how did the city develop?

Oakland County's Troy holds 33.45 square miles of land and an estimated 88,733 residents as of mid-2025, with Sterling Heights on its eastern edge.

Buyers bought the first recorded land in 1819, and Troy Corners grew where a settler purchased 160 acres in what is now north-central Troy. A township formed in 1827, and pieces of it later went to Birmingham, Clawson and Royal Oak. The rest became the city in 1955, partly to keep neighbors from taking more territory. The city is named for Troy, New York, because many early settlers came from New York. Government is council-manager, with a mayor and six council members who appoint a city manager to run daily operations. Growth was sharp: 19,402 people in 1960, 39,419 in 1970, and 87,294 at the 2020 Census.

In the 48098 ZIP code the January average low is 22 degrees Fahrenheit and yearly precipitation totals near 32 inches, so inspectors look closely at roofs and gutters.

Seven districts divide Troy. How do assessments and tax bills affect a Troy seller?

  • Summer bill: goes out July 1 and is clear of penalty through September 1. A 4% charge follows, with half a percent monthly starting October 1.

Homeowners who are 62 or older, disabled or veterans, with income of $40,000 or below, may defer to April 30 by applying through September 15.

Under Michigan law the buyer's taxable value uncaps the year after a transfer. Prorations are set by contract, and the Treasurer's Office at 248.524.3333 can describe the amount due on a given date.

What does selling in Oakland County cost at the Register of Deeds?

Transfer tax is the seller's, due within 15 days of delivery of the deed (MCL 207.523). The state share is $3.75 per $500 (MCL 207.525). MCL 207.504 sets the county share at 55 cents per $500 where a county has fewer than 2,000,000 residents, so confirm the Oakland County figure with the register before closing.

The Register of Deeds answers at 248-858-0597 or deeds@oaklandcountymi.gov, on weekdays, with counter hours starting at 8:30 in the morning. It files deeds, mortgages and foreclosure records, and its Super Index lets you pull recorded documents back to January 1, 1964.

Gifts to children and grandchildren, deeds in foreclosure and court orders with no stated price are exempt under MCL 207.526, and the deed must name the exemption on its face.

What Troy property rules should be settled before showings?

Code Enforcement publishes the complaints it handles most often. A quick walk around the lot can head off a notice during your listing.

  • Lawn grass and weeds stay under 8 inches between May 1 and October 31, including the strip to the road.
  • Snow over 2 inches and ice come off public sidewalks within 24 hours after a storm.
  • Vehicles kept on private land must carry current plates and run, and RVs cannot sit on the street.
  • Temporary signs are allowed on private property, while signs in the public right-of-way are removed.
  • Bins go to the curb after 5 p.m. the day before pickup, and branches near sidewalks need trimming to 8 feet.

Keep open house and yard signs on your own lot. Two more rules matter to some sellers: one commercial pickup or cargo van may sit on private property in a one-family district, and home businesses are allowed in one- and two-family districts under conditions, so a buyer planning to work from the house should call Code Enforcement first.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 median for owner-occupied homes is $420,300. Individual houses vary with age, lot and district.

Summer bills are payable until September 1 and winter bills until February 14. Anything unpaid on March 1 goes to Oakland County.

For the buyer, yes. Taxable value uncaps in the calendar year after a transfer of ownership.

Most houses are in Troy School District, but Avondale, Birmingham, Bloomfield Hills, Lamphere, Royal Oak and Warren Consolidated also cover parts of the city.

With the Oakland County Register of Deeds at 248-858-0597. Transfer tax is collected unless the deed cites an exemption.

  • Before listing, ask the Building Division whether any permit on the address is still open.
  • Patios, playground equipment and backboards need no building permit but must satisfy zoning.
  • Poured concrete without footings falls under the Engineering Department's right-of-way rules, reachable at (248) 871-2560.

How does the tax calendar affect a seller's closing?

Farmington Hills mails its summer bill June 30 and its winter bill November 30. Summer taxes may be paid July 1 through August 31, winter taxes from December 1 to mid-February, and the city adds a 4% penalty after each window. Balances that remain open at the city's March deadline pass to the Oakland County Treasurer. The city's Treasury and Assessing offices answer at 248-871-2480 and 248-871-2470.

Owners who live in the house and are at least 62, disabled, or an eligible veteran or surviving spouse may apply to defer summer taxes if household income is under a set limit. The 2026 form used $40,000. The title company prorates the current bill between you and the buyer, and a payoff letter from Treasury confirms nothing from a prior year remains.

What transfer costs should a Farmington Hills seller budget for?

Michigan levies a county tax of 55 cents and a state tax of $3.75 on every $500 of price, a rate pair set out in MCL 207.504 and 207.525. Sellers owe both. A house changing hands near the city's median value of $354,500 produces about $3,050, a figure the settlement statement will confirm.

After closing, the buyer reports the sale to the city assessor within 45 days. Taxable value then resets to the state equalized value (MCL 211.27a), which is why a buyer's first full tax bill can look steep beside the seller's capped one.

How do schools and commuting routes influence who buys?

Nearly all of the city belongs to Farmington Public Schools. Small corners fall within Clarenceville and Walled Lake Consolidated, and Oakland Early College is a West Bloomfield program located here. North Farmington High School and Farmington Central High School operate within the city limits. Harrison High School closed in 2019 and became a community center called The Hawk. Oakland Community College keeps its Orchard Ridge campus in Farmington Hills.

Drivers rely on M-5, I-696 and I-275 along with Orchard Lake Road and 12 Mile Road, and SMART runs the local buses. According to the city's 2019 financial report, the largest employers include Beaumont Hospital, Robert Bosch, Nissan's technical center, Hitachi and the school district itself. Naming the correct district and the nearest freeway ramp in your sales pitch speaks to the questions most buyers ask first.

When does an as-is cash sale beat a listing here?

A full listing pays off when the house is updated, you can keep it show-ready and a few months of carrying cost is acceptable. A direct as-is sale is stronger when a roof, mechanicals or an estate cleanout stand between you and a market-ready home, or when a relocation date is fixed.

  • Registered rentals with a current certificate may attract landlords looking for ready income.
  • Houses with open permits may be better sold as-is than corrected under deadline.
  • Sellers who still live in the house can compare a cash closing date against a financed buyer's timeline.

Ask for any offer in writing, and compare net proceeds after transfer tax, prorated taxes and credits.

Frequently asked questions

Will open permits block my sale?

They may, since lenders and buyers' inspectors can ask for proof that finished work was permitted. The Building Division at (248) 871-2450 can tell you whether any permit on your address remains open.

Who is responsible for the Michigan transfer tax?

The seller, under the state act. Together the state and county rates come to $4.30 per $500 of price, and the county treasurer collects it after the deed is delivered.

My tenant rents the house. Does the city inspection follow the house to the new owner?

Ask Planning and Community Development. The city registers single-family rentals and inspects them every three years, so the buyer will want the certificate of compliance history.

Which dates matter for tax payments?

Summer bills are payable July 1 through August 31 and winter bills from December 1 to mid-February. A 4% penalty follows each window, and unpaid balances go to the Oakland County Treasurer.

Why would the new owner's tax bill be higher than mine?

A sale resets taxable value to the state equalized value in the following year. Your bill reflected annual caps, while the buyer's starts from the full figure. Assessing at 248-871-2470 can quote the parcel's numbers.

What is the first thing to know about selling a house in Westland?

Before anything else, a Westland seller needs a Certificate of Approval from the city. Every house that is sold or transferred must have one before the residential sale closes, so the certificate sets the pace for the whole deal. The Building Division handles it, and the seller normally opens the file.

Westland is in Wayne County, roughly 18 miles west of downtown Detroit. Deeds for Westland houses go to the Wayne County Register of Deeds, whose appointment system, fees and tax-certification step differ from those in Macomb or Kent counties.

How did Westland grow into the city it is now?

Nankin Township covered this ground until May 16, 1966, when its voters chose to form the City of Westland. The township had reached about 70,000 residents by 1960, the biggest township in Michigan. The vote came after Livonia tried to annex the site of the Westland Shopping Center, which opened in 1965.

Norwayne, one of the oldest subdivisions, was built right after World War II as temporary housing for veterans working in nearby factories. Westland now spans 20.4 square miles, and every census since 1970 has counted between roughly 84,000 and 87,000 residents.

Ford Road (M-153) crosses central Westland. Wayne County's Hines Park lies along the northern edge, and the city maintains its own neighborhood parks. Garbage goes out weekly in the black bin, and the blue recycling bin is picked up every second week.

Which school districts serve Westland addresses?

The Wayne-Westland Community School District covers most of the city. John Glenn High School serves central Westland and part of the north, and some southern blocks feed Wayne Memorial High School in the city of Wayne. The far northern edge belongs to Livonia Public Schools, whose Churchill and Franklin high schools take those students.

Corners of southeastern Westland are divided between Romulus Community Schools and the Taylor School District, after the Inkster district was dissolved. Assignments can change within a block, so ask the district about the exact address and pass the answer to the buyer.

What do Census numbers show for Westland homeowners?

Census estimates put Westland at 82,333 people on July 1, 2025, which is 3.6 percent less than the 2020 base of 85,409. The 2020 count found 39,633 housing units, 4.9 percent of them empty. Between 2020 and 2024 the bureau tallied 35,932 households with 2.30 people apiece.

Owners live in only 61.3 percent of Westland homes, a smaller share than in many Michigan suburbs, which is one reason the city's rental rules draw attention. Homes lived in by their owners have a median value of $184,600. Renters pay $1,158 a month at the median, and household income has a median of $62,076. Owners with a mortgage pay $1,360 a month at the median.

How does Westland's Certificate of Approval work?

The seller sends the Building Division (36300 Warren Road, phone 734-467-3210, open weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) a Home Sale or Transfer application. An inspector then walks the house against the property maintenance code. Inspections can be booked online, by email to building@cityofwestland.com, by phone or at the counter.

  • A mechanical contractor registered with Westland tests the furnace or boiler and signs the city's own certification form.
  • If the home has a fireplace, a chimney contractor files a safety inspection report as well.
  • A seller who completes the process receives a certificate that stays valid for six months.
  • A seller who stops short leaves a second path: the buyer pays $80 for an Approval Letter to Close, files a Remaining Violations Disclosure Form along with the signed purchase agreement, and then gets ninety days to fix the items and book the final inspection.

That second path can suit an as-is cash purchase, because the closing proceeds with the open items and the repairs shift to the buyer.

Do open permits or rentals complicate a Westland sale?

They can. The Building Division issues the permits that homeowners most often skip: re-roofing, decks, fences, fireplaces, garages, pools, kitchen expansions and basement finishing all need one, and electrical, plumbing and heating work each take a separate trade permit. A housing inspector walking the house for the Certificate of Approval is likely to ask about any of that work, so gather permit numbers and final approvals before the visit.

Westland also runs a rental program, with a Rental Registration Application on the Building Division's forms list. An owner selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Building Division at 734-467-3210 how the registration and the sale certificate interact, and whether the rental registration is current before the house goes under contract.

Westland's Planning and Building Department also lists a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy request form, a separate route used while work is still unfinished. Ask the department whether that form applies to your situation before you promise a buyer a closing date.

What does a Westland sale cost in city and county charges?

The city's fee varies with building type. On the county side, recording a deed costs $26 plus a $4 state survey fee. The county says its schedule of January 1, 2026 was its first increase since 1996. Deeds and land contracts also need Wayne County treasurer certification unless an exemption applies.

Westland sale charges. Sources: City of Westland Home Sale or Transfer application and Wayne County Register of Deeds.

Wayne County restates the combined rate as $8.60 per $1,000, payable at the recording counter.

How do I record a deed with the Wayne County Register of Deeds?

Wayne County has served customers by appointment only since October 1, 2025. A visitor with up to five documents gets a 20 minute slot, while the 45 minute slots go to people filing five to 25. Book on 313-224-5860, or call 313-224-5851 with recording questions.

The county's list of common rejections includes:

  • A photocopied signature where an original is needed.
  • A deed that names neither a consideration amount nor an exemption statute.
  • A first page lacking the 2.5 inch top margin, or type below 10 point.
  • Social Security digits left visible.
  • A warranty deed without the county treasurer's certification.

Transfer tax is accepted as cash, check or money order. Cards work for other charges with matching ID, but American Express and Discover do not. A check more than $25 over the amount due is returned unprocessed.

Is there any way to close a Westland sale without the seller finishing the city inspection?

Yes. The buyer pays $80 for an Approval Letter to Close and signs the violations disclosure form with the purchase agreement. That opens a ninety-day period to complete repairs and pass the final inspection.

What fee does Westland charge on a Home Sale or Transfer application?

The rate is $250 for single-family houses, $475 for duplexes and $900 for multi-family buildings, according to the city's application dated Rev. 7-1-26. The seller files it with the Building Division.

How long is a Westland Certificate of Approval valid?

Six months from issue, for a seller who completes the inspection. The city's furnace or boiler certification must be on file before final approval is granted.

Who pays Michigan transfer tax when a Westland house sells?

The seller. Wayne County lists $0.55 per $500 for the county and $3.75 per $500 for the state, collected as the deed is recorded.

Does Wayne County require an appointment to record a Westland deed?

Yes, since October 1, 2025. Daily slots start at 8:00 a.m. and the last begins at 3:50 p.m. For property tax amounts and due dates, ask the Westland Finance Department before closing.

Why do Flint sales hinge on condition and clear title?

Flint homes sell for far less than homes elsewhere in Michigan, so a seller's outcome depends on repair costs, liens and ownership history more than on the asking price. Flint is the Genesee County seat, about 66 miles northwest of Detroit on the Flint River, and the Census Bureau estimated 79,306 residents on July 1, 2025.

A Flint owner has three paths: an agent listing, a direct sale to a neighbor or investor, or a buyer who pays cash and takes the house untouched. The sections below set each path against the city's rental ordinance, its water billing rule, county tax foreclosure and the figures behind local values.

How has Flint's history shaped its housing?

Fur trader Jacob Smith founded a trading post here in 1819, the village incorporated in 1855, and lumber and carriage building turned into automobile manufacturing. Buick moved to Flint, Chevrolet built its first plant here, and General Motors was founded in the city in 1908. Local GM employment peaked near 80,000 in 1978 and fell below 8,000 by 2010.

Population followed the jobs down. It reached about 197,000 in 1960 and measured 81,252 in the 2020 Census. The housing stock was built for that larger workforce, so a seller here is often marketing an older house to a smaller pool of buyers than the city once had.

  • Older houses can carry repair items such as roofs, wiring and plumbing that a buyer's inspector will list.
  • The Land Bank holds vacant lots and houses, so some occupied blocks sit beside empty parcels.
  • Tax foreclosure has shaped ownership here, so parcel history deserves a look before you sign anything.
  • The city lived through a lead-in-water emergency from 2014 to 2019, and Wikipedia reports a new water source plus copper service pipes at nearly every home since, so buyers may ask what work was done at your address.

How low are Flint home values, and who owns the houses?

A city where renters nearly match owners and where the middle owner-occupied house is valued at $53,500.

Which Flint neighborhoods and landmarks matter to buyers?

Flint's neighborhoods are grouped around downtown, which is centered on Saginaw Street south of the river. Carriage Town and the Grand Traverse Street District hold preserved Victorian houses just west of downtown. East of I-475, Central Park and Fairfield Village sit between the University of Michigan-Flint and Mott Community College. East Village and the College Cultural Neighborhood on the east side are described as more stable, and the west side includes Mott Park and the Woodcroft Estates.

Public schools are run by Flint Community Schools, which operates ten elementary schools, one middle school and Flint Southwestern Academy. Catholic and charter schools also serve the city. Kettering University, UM-Flint and Mott Community College are all in or beside the city's core.

What are Flint's rental rules, and do they affect a sale?

They do if the house has tenants. Flint's rental ordinance requires rental properties to be registered with the city and certified after an inspection. A December 2023 city memo put the single-family registration at a one-time $250 and the inspection at $225 every three years, and it said tenants make up nearly half of Flint households. Landlords must provide heat from October 1 through March 31.

The same memo explains a water rule that surprises owners: the city prefers water accounts in the owner's name, and unpaid water bills become a lien that can be added to the property tax bill. Before selling a rental, make sure the water account is paid and call the Building and Safety Inspections Division at 810-766-7284 to learn where the certification stands. Fees change, so request the current schedule.

How does Genesee County tax foreclosure affect Flint sellers?

A delinquent tax bill can move a house into county tax foreclosure, and that is a real risk for owners of inherited or vacant property. The Genesee County Land Bank takes in properties through the tax foreclosure process: houses that go unsold at the public auction and are not claimed by the state or a local government are transferred from the County Treasurer to the Land Bank at the end of each calendar year.

Owners in the city can check parcel ownership through the city's property lookup, and a parcel listed under Genesee County LRC Inc or the Genesee County Treasurer is held by the Land Bank. For a seller, the lesson is simple: pay or arrange the back taxes before the foreclosure clock runs out, because a sale closed on time keeps the equity that an auction would not.

  • Get the exact tax balance from the county treasurer before signing a purchase contract.
  • Unpaid water bills can sit on the tax roll as well.
  • Ask the title company to pull liens early so surprises do not delay closing.
