What does the Michigan transfer tax cost on a Flint house?

Two Michigan transfer taxes apply: 55 cents for the county plus $3.75 for the state on every $500 of price, per MCL 207.504 and 207.525. The seller bears them, and payment goes to the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523).

A sale at Flint's middle value of $53,500 would owe about $460, and the settlement statement will give the real figure. The buyer then notifies the city assessor within 45 days so that taxable value can reset the next year (MCL 211.27a).

When does an as-is sale beat a listing in Flint?

A sound house on a stable block can do well with an agent, provided the buyer's appraisal supports the contract price. When repairs would cost more than they add, or a lien, code order or tenant dispute clouds the deal, selling the house untouched removes most of the friction.

  • An agent listing suits a move-in-ready house when you can wait through loan approval.
  • An as-is buyer suits a house whose repair quotes outrun its likely sale price.
  • A neighbor suits an empty lot beside their home, a logic the Land Bank applies when it sells side lots.

Ask for proof of funds, read the closing date clause, and compare offers by what you keep after liens and costs.

Frequently asked questions

Can unpaid property taxes be settled out of a Flint sale?

Usually yes, if closing happens before the county finishes foreclosure. The title agent subtracts the balance from your proceeds, and the Genesee County Treasurer can confirm the payoff and the foreclosure timeline.

Do unpaid Flint water bills follow the house?

They can. City rules let delinquent water charges become a lien added to the property tax bill, so a title agent will usually want the account paid before closing.

What does Flint expect of a landlord?

Rentals must be registered and certified after an inspection, repeated every three years, and landlords must supply heat from October 1 through March 31. Request the current fee schedule from Building and Safety Inspections.

What would Michigan transfer tax come to at Flint's typical home value?

About $460 on $53,500, combining 55 cents per $500 for the county with $3.75 per $500 for the state. Your settlement statement shows the exact amount.

What is the Genesee County Land Bank?

A county entity that receives tax-foreclosed properties that fail to sell at auction. It sells houses and lots, offers side lots to neighboring owners and demolishes dangerous structures as funding allows.

What should a seller know about Wyoming, Michigan?

Wyoming, with about 78,600 residents, is a Kent County city on the southwest side of the Grand Rapids area, and only Grand Rapids itself is larger in West Michigan. Selling a house here involves the city Assessor's Office for transfer paperwork, the Kent County Register of Deeds in downtown Grand Rapids for recording, and a few city codes that surface during a buyer's inspection.

This page covers Wyoming, Michigan, which has no tie to the state of Wyoming. The sections run in the order of a sale: how the city formed, who lives and works here, the city's rules, and the filings that follow closing.

How did Wyoming develop into a city of its own?

Settlers came in 1832 and built mills on Buck Creek, and by 1834 the settlement was known as Little Prairie. It became Wyoming Township in 1848 after separating from Byron Township. For roughly a century it fed produce and goods into Grand Rapids, until the Grand Rapids, Holland and Chicago Railway brought suburban building.

Grandville incorporated in 1933 and a General Motors stamping plant opened, and the resulting annexation fights ended when Wyoming became a city in 1959. The 28th Street strip grew into a regional shopping and movie destination around Rogers Plaza and Studio 28. It declined in the 1980s while new building moved southwest toward RiverTown Crossings. The GM plant shut in 2009, and recent efforts center on the City Center project along 28th Street and the 74-acre former plant property, called Site 36.

Wyoming has 21 parks on about 665 acres and ties into the Kent Trails bike network. The 2002 Wyoming Public Library is city-owned and operated by the Kent District Library. On the last weekend of August, the 28th Street Metro Cruise brings classic cars along a 15 mile route through town.

What drives the Wyoming housing market?

Manufacturing is the largest local industry. The city's 2025 annual financial report puts these employers on top:

  • Gordon Food Service, 5,000 workers.
  • Metro Health Hospital, 3,000.
  • GM Components Holdings, 1,200.
  • ABC Technologies, 650, and Benteler, 580.

US-131 cuts north and south through the middle of the city, M-11 (28th Street) crosses it east to west, and M-6 touches the southern edge. Eight of The Rapid's routes serve Wyoming. Workers here report a mean commute of 21.9 minutes.

Eight school districts overlap the city: Wyoming Public Schools in the center, Godwin Heights in the northeast, Godfrey-Lee in the north, Kelloggsville in the southeast, Kentwood below 56th Street and east of the tracks, Grandville in the southwest, Byron Center near Metro Health, and a sliver of Grand Rapids Public Schools. Verify the district by street address.

What do Census figures say about Wyoming homeowners?

The 2025 estimate of 78,588 residents is 2.7 percent higher than the 2020 base, up from 72,125 in 2010. Across 2020 through 2024, Wyoming had 29,417 households of about 2.61 people, and 67.1 percent of them were owners.

Homes occupied by their owners have a median value of $225,200. Gross rent has a median of $1,196, household income $73,677, and 25.5 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree. A typical owner with a mortgage spends $1,398 a month.

Which Wyoming city rules matter to a seller?

Every rental in Wyoming has to be registered and certified, and the BS&A Online portal shows the status for any address. If you are selling a rented house, check that the certificate is current before a buyer finds an open violation. A short-term rental of 27 days or less must also register, at no cost and without an inspection.

Inspections, at 1155 28th St. SW (616-530-7285), issues building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing permits. Homeowners can apply online with no account, and most residential permits take one to two weeks. A buyer's inspector may flag these maintenance items:

  • Lawn grass or weeds over 10 inches.
  • Trash containers visible from the front of the house.
  • Cars on unpaved ground, or unlicensed vehicles outside a garage.
  • Fences in the required front yard taller than 36 inches.

Backyard hens are allowed by permit. The permit is free, caps a household at four chickens, bans roosters and free-range birds, and starts with a two-week comment period for adjacent neighbors, so a buyer who plans to keep hens should ask whether a permit exists for the house. Owners who want to split or combine a lot file a land division application with the Assessor's Office by the first Monday in October for it to take effect in the next tax year.

What must be filed with the Wyoming Assessor after a sale?

The assessor tracks roughly 25,000 parcels and values them at 50 percent of the usual selling price. Taxable value is capped: it cannot grow each year by more than inflation or 5 percent, whichever is smaller. After a sale, the cap lifts in the following year and taxable value rises to match assessed value.

Each change of ownership goes on a Property Transfer Affidavit, which the assessor's page says must be filed within 45 days. The title company typically hands over the form at closing. Leaving it out can trigger back taxes, penalties and interest running from the transfer date.

The Register of Deeds for Kent County works from 300 Monroe Avenue NW in downtown Grand Rapids and takes cash, checks or money orders made out to the Register of Deeds. Its published charges:

  • $30 for a deed, mortgage or other instrument.
  • $5 per deed for treasurer's tax certification of warranty deeds and land contracts, covering up to 25 parcels.
  • $1.10 per thousand of consideration for the county transfer tax.
  • $7.50 per thousand of consideration for the state transfer tax.

Kent County says the seller or grantor owes the tax and that mortgages owe none. The deed states the full consideration, or a Real Estate Transfer Valuation Affidavit is filed at no charge. The office will not supply blank deeds or advise on drafting, so work with a title company or attorney.

What is the deadline for a Property Transfer Affidavit after a Wyoming sale?

The City of Wyoming Assessor's Office says it is due within 45 days of the transfer. The title company normally supplies the form at closing, and a missed filing can bring back taxes with penalties and interest.

Will the property tax bill on a Wyoming house change after a sale?

For the new owner, yes. The cap on taxable value resets to assessed value the year following a sale, and Wyoming assesses at 50 percent of the usual selling price.

Does a rented Wyoming house need a certificate before it sells?

The city requires every rental to be registered and certified, so a landlord should make sure the certificate is current. The Inspections Department, 616-530-7285, can check the status.

Which office records a Wyoming deed?

The Kent County Register of Deeds, 300 Monroe Avenue NW, Grand Rapids. It charges $30 per document, and a warranty deed also needs the $5 treasurer certification.

Can I still appeal a Wyoming assessment after the March Board of Review?

Yes, through the Michigan Tax Tribunal, which must receive residential appeals by July 31. The July and December boards only correct clerical errors and mutual mistakes and consider certain exemptions.

What is different about a Rochester Hills sale?

Rochester Hills is a high-value Oakland County suburb, yet the paperwork is modest: a deed filed with the county, two affidavits for the city's Assessing Department, and a treasurer's tax certificate. Most of the work happens at the county and state level.

Downtown Detroit is roughly 25 miles south. European settlement began in 1817, Avon Township was organized in 1835, and a 1984 charter vote turned the township into the City of Rochester Hills. The older city of Rochester incorporated in 1967 and remains a separate municipality, a distinction buyers often blur.

How did Rochester Hills become a city?

Rochester Hills incorporated late and after a long fight over its boundaries. The Potawatomi lived along the Clinton River and Paint Creek until the 1807 Treaty of Detroit ceded southeast Michigan, and the township that followed adopted a charter in 1948 under the Home Rule Act. A post office called Brooklands opened that same year between Auburn Road and Hamlin Road.

After Rochester became its own city in 1967, its residents stopped paying township property tax. Three proposed city charters failed between 1969 and 1971, and a dispute over a 1974 annexation by Rochester stayed in the courts until 1981. In May 1984 township voters approved a charter, and the new city took the name Rochester Hills over the alternative Avon Hills. When the title company asks for a legal description, match it to the parcel number on your tax bill.

The land area is 32.80 square miles, about 2,326 residents live on each, and the July 2025 estimate of 77,539 sits 1.6 percent above the 76,321 counted at the 2020 base.

Which schools serve Rochester Hills addresses?

Rochester Community Schools serve most of the city, with Rochester Adams High School, Rochester High School and Stoney Creek High School all inside the city limits. Part of Rochester Hills falls in the Avondale School District instead, where many addresses are zoned to Deer Field Elementary in the city, while others go to Auburn Elementary in Auburn Hills or Woodland Elementary in Troy.

All Avondale residents attend Avondale Middle School in Rochester Hills and Avondale High School in Auburn Hills. Addresses in different parts of the city can belong to different districts, so get an official boundary check before a listing names a school.

Colleges add a buyer group: Oakland University and Rochester Christian University both offer programs here. The city runs the Rochester Hills Public Library and, by contract, lets residents of the city of Rochester and Oakland Township use it.

What surrounds Rochester Hills?

Rochester Hills is rolling, as the name suggests. Elevation climbs from about 690 feet in the southeast to 1,032 feet in the northwest, and the Clinton River and Paint Creek were the water sources that drew the first settlers.

Its boundaries run as follows:

  • Troy to the south, along South Boulevard.
  • Shelby Township in Macomb County to the east, along Dequindre Road, with the city of Rochester partly on the eastern edge.

The city keeps no police department of its own, and the Oakland County Sheriff's Office provides police service. The 52nd District Court's third division sits in the city too. When a buyer asks about services, send them to the city's website and the sheriff's office.

Which forms go to Rochester Hills assessing after closing?

Two documents go to the Assessing Department at 1000 Rochester Hills Drive: a Property Transfer Affidavit and, for an owner-occupant, a Principal Residence Exemption affidavit. The city expects the closing agent to give the buyer both, and they can be mailed or dropped off during weekday office hours.

The exemption lifts up to 18 mills of school tax off a bill when the owner lives there as a main residence. Sellers should ask Assessing for the rescission form so the exemption on the old home ends cleanly. The department also administers disabled veteran and poverty exemptions, and the poverty request has to be refiled every year.

A buyer who wants a quick tax estimate can follow the city's rule of thumb, which halves the estimated value and applies the current millage rate, or ask Assessing to run it. An owner who disputes a value gets one chance a year: the March Board of Review, after the February notice.

What does the Oakland County deed filing involve?

A deed filed with the Oakland County Register of Deeds costs $30, which already contains the state's $4 survey surcharge. A discharge or assignment that cites several earlier recordings adds $3 for each extra reference, and copies run $1 a page.

The county treasurer must certify warranty deeds and land contracts first, for $5. When you mail the deed, the Register of Deeds can obtain that certificate if your payment includes the extra $5. Expect about two weeks to get a hand-delivered document back and two to four weeks by mail.

The county's fee page states both transfer tax shares: $0.55 per $500 for the county and $3.75 per $500 for the state. A deed with consideration under $100 is exempt, and any other claimed exemption must appear on the deed. The seller carries the bill under MCL 207.523.

What does the Rochester Hills tax calendar mean for my closing?

The summer bill covers school and county levies only. It is payable July 1 through September 14, and 1 percent interest starts September 15. Winter bills open December 1 and fall due in mid-February.

  • The city shows February 16, 2027 as the winter due date for the 2026 tax year, with a 3 percent penalty shortly after.
  • Anything still owed turns delinquent on March 2 and moves to the Oakland County Treasurer.
  • Postmarks do not count, so pay in person or online close to a deadline.
  • E-check payments are free online, while cards and mobile wallets add a 2.75 percent processing charge.

The winter bill adds the city's own levy for police and fire services, roads and the library, so a fall or winter closing can land before it is paid. Have the title company say who pays it and how it is credited, and use the Treasury tax look-up to see each parcel's status.

Where is a Rochester Hills deed recorded?

At the Oakland County Register of Deeds, for $30 including the $4 survey surcharge. Warranty deeds first need a $5 treasurer certificate.

Must a Rochester Hills house pass a city inspection before closing?

Ask the city's Building Department whether one applies to your address, and do it before you pick a closing date. The Assessing Department only handles tax forms.

What paperwork does a Rochester Hills buyer owe the city?

A Property Transfer Affidavit, and an exemption affidavit for a buyer who will live there. Both go to Assessing at 1000 Rochester Hills Drive.

What are the tax deadlines in Rochester Hills?

September 14 for summer and mid-February for winter, listed as February 16, 2027 for the 2026 bill. Oakland County takes over unpaid balances on March 2.

Who covers transfer tax on a Rochester Hills sale?

The seller. The county lists $3.75 per $500 for the state portion and $0.55 per $500 for its own.

How does the new inspection rule change a Southfield sale?

Southfield residential sales now run through a point-of-sale inspection, and that step sets the pace of a closing. City Council approved the program in April 2026 as Ordinance 1835, so schedule the inspection before you commit to a closing date.

The city is an inner-ring Detroit suburb in Oakland County, with a July 2025 Census estimate of 76,111 residents. Owners live in just 53.4 percent of housing units, the lowest share among the four cities in the same Census table, so rentals are common.

A seller can go three ways:

  • Private sale: you find the buyer and manage the contract with a title company.
  • Cash sale as-is: the buyer takes the house with whatever the inspection cites. Settle who pays for those repairs before you sign.

Because the program is new, ask the Building Department how it treats a sale that is already under contract, and keep the inspection report with your closing file.

How does the Southfield point-of-sale inspection work?

The Building and Safety Engineering department inspects the house and issues a Certificate of Occupancy after violations are cleared. Its Point of Sale packet walks through the steps, and you apply on the city's online BS&A portal.

  • The packet prints $190 for the resale inspection: $40 to apply, $50 for the certificate and $100 for the building trade, reinspection included.
  • Payment comes first. Staff then book the visit within 14 days of the payment date.
  • A person has to stay at the house for the whole window, either 9:30 to 12:30 or 12:30 to 3:30.
  • Sellers can repair the listed items and ask for a follow-up visit, which the fee covers.
  • Alternatively, buyer and seller both sign an Affidavit to Assume Resale Violations before closing, and the buyer gets 30 days afterward to finish the work.

The affidavit form calls for a performance bond sized to the repairs and bars occupancy until the work passes reinspection. Life safety items must be corrected before anyone moves in. The Building Department answers questions at 248-796-4100.

Southfield lies about 15 miles northwest of downtown Detroit and holds 26.25 square miles of land. Eight Mile Road bounds it on the south, Inkster Road on the west and Greenfield Road on the east, while the north edge follows roughly Thirteen Mile Road. Lathrup Village, a separate city, sits as an enclave inside the eastern part.

Surveyors laid out the area in 1817 and it became a township in 1830. It incorporated as a city on April 28, 1958, and population jumped from 31,531 in 1960 to 69,298 in 1970. Wikipedia calls it a historic center of mid-century modern architecture in Michigan.

Offices anchor the economy. About 27 million square feet of office space and more than 100 Fortune 500 companies with offices here, plus several TV stations and Lawrence Technological University. Northland Center, among the first shopping malls in the country, opened in 1954 and closed in 2015, and its site has been redeveloped as a mixed-use project.

The 2010 census counted 71,739 residents and the 2020 census counted 76,618, so the city grew over the decade. The 2020 median age was 44.0 years, and about 40.9 percent of households were one person living alone.

Southfield City Centre, a mixed-use district near the I-696 and M-10 interchange with offices, a private university and residential neighborhoods, was created in 1992 as a special assessment district. The Civic Center complex, which holds City Hall and the police headquarters, dates to 1964, and an expanded public library opened on its grounds in 2003. Municipal parks and recreation centers were largely built in the 1970s, and Beech Woods Recreation Center and John Grace Community Center are among them.

A rented house adds scheduling work, since someone has to be present for the inspection. A vacant house should be secured, heated in cold months and cleared of debris, so the inspector sees its true condition.

What is the Kalamazoo housing market like for a seller?

Kalamazoo is the biggest of these four cities and has the most renters. Mid-2025 estimates count 72,683 people, and just 42.3 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. Sellers here often hold a house near a campus, a former rental or a long-held family home, and the right route depends on which applies.

A listing, a private sale and a cash purchase all pass through the same city desks: the assessor, the treasurer and the rental inspection team. After those are settled, the deed goes to the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds, which holds records dating to 1831.

How did Kalamazoo grow, and where do homes sit in the city?

Titus Bronson settled the site in 1829, and the town bore his name until 1836, when it was renamed for the river. Kalamazoo spans 25.11 square miles along a bend in the Kalamazoo River, with a flat northeastern section in the valley and low hills toward the west and south. 22 neighborhoods, many with a neighborhood association that works with the city's Neighborhood Development Division.

Kalamazoo sits midway between Detroit and Chicago on I-94 and lies 50 miles south of Grand Rapids. US 131, M-96 and M-343 tie it to nearby towns. The downtown Amtrak station anchors the 110 mph stretch of the Wolverine line between Porter, Indiana and Albion, Michigan. Flights use Kalamazoo/Battle Creek International Airport at the south end of the city. Weather runs hot and humid in summer with lake-effect snow in winter, and a major tornado crossed downtown in 1980.

Who lives in Kalamazoo homes?

Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024 describe a college town with mid-range prices:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $179,000.
  • Households: 29,523, with 2.25 persons each.
  • Typical rent: $1,078.
  • Adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or more: 38.5 percent.
  • Share of people at the same address a year earlier: 75.9 percent, the lowest of the four cities, which fits a place with many students and renters.

Estimates show a 1.2 percent dip from 2020 to 2025, so the market is steady. A buyer who plans to rent your house must register it with the city.

How does the Kalamazoo Promise figure into a sale?

Most of the city is served by Kalamazoo Public Schools, with small sections in Parchment, Comstock and Portage districts. Every resident graduate of Kalamazoo Public Schools has been eligible, since the class of 2006, for a scholarship covering up to 100 percent of tuition and mandatory fees for four years at any public university or community college in Michigan. The program is the Kalamazoo Promise, and buyers with children often ask about it.

The city also hosts Western Michigan University, Kalamazoo College (founded 1833), Kalamazoo Valley Community College and Davenport University, along with the WMU Homer Stryker School of Medicine, open since 2014. Houses near those campuses are more likely to have a rental history, which brings the city's rental rules into play.

Which Kalamazoo neighborhoods and employers shape buyer interest?

The city is commonly divided into 22 neighborhoods, and many have an association that works with the city on projects funded by programs such as Community Development Block Grants. Western Michigan University's West Campus, just west of downtown, holds the largest concentration of students, while Kalamazoo College sits on a hill opposite the university's original campus. Downtown centers on the Kalamazoo Mall, created in 1959 when part of Burdick Street closed to cars.

Local employers include Bell's Brewery, begun in 1985 as the Kalamazoo Brewing Company, and the A.M. Todd Company, a producer of peppermint oil and other flavorings headquartered in the city. Put the block, the walk to campus or downtown, and any association in your description, because buyers shop by neighborhood.

How does Kalamazoo's rental certification affect selling a rental?

The city requires registration and certification of every rental. After a passing inspection against the Housing Code (Chapter 17 of the city code), the owner receives a Certificate of Compliance. Inspectors may return at least every 28 months, and a courtesy notice arrives four months before expiry. Book the inspection about three months ahead and schedule any reinspection within 10 days.

Kalamazoo Certificate of Compliance lengths and conditions
CertificateWho qualifies
28 monthsStandard certificate for any rental, and the fallback when a property misses a longer one
40 monthsRenewals issued before the old certificate expires, with no appearance tickets or enforcement letters and six or fewer documented violations last cycle
52 monthsRenewals after two consecutive 40-month certificates, with no conditions and four or fewer trash or nuisance violations

Source: City of Kalamazoo Rental Registration Rules and Responsibilities. Give a buyer the certificate's expiration date and any open violations, and ask the rental inspections team to update the owner on the registration form after the sale.

What is the Kalamazoo tax calendar, and who can defer?

The summer bill is mailed by July 1 and due July 31, payable whole or in six monthly installments. Miss the first installment and the city adds a single 3 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest on the first of every month. The winter bill, mailed by December 1, is due February 14 in a single payment. After March 1, unpaid amounts are delinquent and go to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer.

A summer bill can be deferred to the winter date by owners whose household income last year did not exceed $40,000 and who fit one of these groups:

  • Age 62 or older, including an unmarried surviving spouse of someone who was 62 or older.
  • Blind, paraplegic, hemiplegic, quadriplegic, or totally and permanently disabled.
  • An eligible service member, veteran, widow or widower.

Applications reach the City Treasurer by September 15. Owner-occupants can also claim the principal residence exemption, which the city says trims a yearly bill by over 25 percent.

What exemption paperwork changes when I sell in Kalamazoo?

Sellers file a rescission of their principal residence exemption with the assessor, and a buyer who moves in files a new affidavit. Michigan also lets someone who buys a second home keep the exemption on the first for up to 3 years if it is empty, for sale, unleased and not used for business; the city's FAQ says that conditional form must be re-filed each December 31. If you use that option, confirm it with the City Assessor's office before listing.

What would a Kalamazoo deed cost in transfer tax?

Take the median value as a worked example. A $179,000 price is 358 units of $500. State tax is $3.75 a unit (MCL 207.525) and the county adds 55 cents a unit where it has under 2,000,000 residents (MCL 207.504), so the seller owes 358 times $4.30, or $1,539.40, to the county treasurer inside 15 days after delivering the deed. MCL 207.526 exempts gifts to a child or grandchild, court orders that state no price, and deeds that merely confirm existing title.

How often does Kalamazoo inspect a rental?

The city may inspect each rental every 28 months. Owners who renew on time and keep clean records can earn 40 or 52 month certificates with fewer visits.

When are Kalamazoo winter taxes due?

February 14, in one payment. The bill is mailed by December 1, and balances still open on March 1 are delinquent and payable to the Kalamazoo County Treasurer.

Can I defer my Kalamazoo summer tax bill?

Possibly. Household income last year must be at most $40,000, and you must be in a listed group such as 62 or older or disabled. Apply to the City Treasurer by September 15; the summer bill then falls due with the winter bill.

What is the Kalamazoo Promise?

A scholarship for resident graduates of Kalamazoo Public Schools covering up to 100 percent of tuition and mandatory fees for four years at any Michigan public university or community college, starting with the class of 2006.

What is the transfer tax on a $179,000 Kalamazoo sale?

$1,539.40: 358 units of $500 at $3.75 for the state and $0.55 for the county, paid by the seller.

Which selling routes make sense for a Novi homeowner?

Novi owners usually weigh a full-service listing, a private sale, and a quick sale to a buyer who pays without a bank. Each one ends in the same two places: the city assessing office for tax forms, and the Oakland County deed office for the transfer.

The routes differ in how long they take and what you pay out. Showings, a buyer's loan approval and repair negotiations stretch a listing across months. A direct purchase compresses that into one negotiation, so line up the net amount you would receive from each route. The local steps below apply to every route.

Where is Novi and how is it laid out?

Novi is a northwestern Detroit suburb in Oakland County, roughly 25 miles from downtown Detroit. The city spans 31.29 square miles, with 30.25 of land and the rest water. Walled Lake is the largest lake inside the boundary. Interstates 96, 696 and 275 converge here, and M-5 adds another link, which is why a house near one of these roads is a short ride from much of metro Detroit.

Novi Township was organized in 1832. Voters approved a city charter that became effective on February 24, 1969, drawing the city along the lines of the old village. Growth was quick through the later twentieth century, and Twelve Oaks Mall, opened in 1977, turned the Novi Road and I-96 corner into a regional shopping stop.

Most of the city drains to the Rouge River, and parts of the north and west sides drain toward the Huron River. The city's forms page lists a Minor Land Improvement Permit for any change that affects drainage on a property, so a regraded yard or new patio is worth checking against permit records before you list.

Which schools and employers bring buyers to Novi?

Novi Community Schools covers most of the city and operates Novi High School, Novi Middle School and six elementary buildings. The Census Bureau lists 29.2% of Novi residents as foreign-born, and 33.2% of residents aged five and up speak another language at home. Relocating employees from overseas and out of state are part of the buyer pool.

Which tax forms does Novi's assessing office handle at a sale?

Novi's Assessing Department answers at 248-347-0485 and handles four items you will likely touch: the transfer affidavit, the principal residence exemption, protests, and the yearly reappraisal.

  • Transfer affidavit: the city's forms page says state law wants it in hand within 45 days after the date of transfer.
  • Principal residence exemption: this takes up to 18 mills of school operating tax off a homeowner's bill. When the house sells, the owner files the rescission form right away, because penalties and interest run back to the sale date if filing is late.
  • Conditional rescission: someone who moved into a new Michigan home can keep a conditional rescission on the old one for up to three years, as long as it is listed, empty, unrented and unused for business.
  • Board of Review: an assessment protest starts with a petition to the board.

City appraisers walk neighborhoods every year, and the State Tax Commission suggests that assessors inspect 20% of parcels annually, refreshing photos and sometimes measuring. A new deck, finished basement or garage will show up on the record card. Poverty exemption requests go to the July or December board and come with two years of returns and current account statements.

Do permits and occupancy papers matter when a Novi house changes hands?

They do, because buyers and their inspectors ask about work done to the house. Novi publishes separate applications for building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work, and an owner acting as general contractor completes the Homeowner Permit Policy form.

The same page has an occupancy request form for new construction and warns that the Building Department needs two days' notice to process it. A temporary certificate of occupancy runs through the Administrative Board of Appeals. If you pulled permits for a kitchen, furnace, roof or addition, collect the final inspection sign-offs now. The Novi Building Department can supply a copy of any record you cannot locate.

What does the Oakland County deed office do after a Novi closing?

The transfer is recorded at the Oakland County Register of Deeds, reachable at 248-858-0597. Its fee page prices a deed recording at $30.00, a total that folds in a $4 state land-survey charge.

Any deed with a warranty covenant has to be tax certified at the Oakland County Treasurer's Office before recording, and the county lists a $5.00 certificate charge. The closing agent usually walks both steps over. Pages need a 2-1/2 inch blank strip at the top and a half inch elsewhere.

The county also posts its transfer tax: 55 cents for each $500 of consideration goes to the county and $3.75 for each $500 goes to the state. Look for both lines on your closing statement before you sign.

Do Novi sellers have to fix things before closing?

No Novi rule forces repairs before a sale. Unpermitted or unfinished work is the exception, so ask the Building Department about permit history first. A buyer paying without a loan may take the house as it stands, while a lender behind a financed buyer can insist on fixes.

When is the Property Transfer Affidavit due after a Novi sale?

Within 45 days of the transfer, according to Novi's forms page. It goes to the city assessor, and your closing agent may be able to submit it for you.

Does the principal residence exemption stay with the house after a Novi sale?

No. The seller must rescind it with the assessor as soon as the home is sold, rented or left, and late filing triggers penalties and interest back to that date. A conditional rescission can last up to three years on a vacant, listed, unrented former home.

Which office takes the deed after a Novi closing?

The Oakland County Register of Deeds, not the city. Recording costs $30.00, and a warranty deed first needs a $5.00 treasurer's tax certificate, so most sellers leave the filing to their closing agent.

Which school district will a Novi buyer be in?

Most of Novi is in Novi Community Schools. The south side is in Northville Public Schools, a section is in Walled Lake Consolidated Schools and a small western piece is in South Lyon Community Schools, so check the district for your address.

A Pontiac owner can hire an agent, sell without one, or deal with a company that buys houses directly. Pontiac is also the Oakland County seat, and the county's deed office and treasurer handle the recording side of every sale in the city.

The house usually points to the route. A sound property with clean permit records suits a public listing. A property with deferred repairs, an occupant, tax trouble or an inherited title often moves faster with a buyer who takes it as it stands. Whichever way you go, put terms on paper and have a closing agent check ownership and any recorded liens.

What should a seller know about Pontiac's layout and past?

Pontiac covers 20.29 square miles, with 19.97 of them land. Auburn Hills borders it on the east and north, Lake Angelus lies to the north, Waterford Township sits west and Bloomfield Township south. The Clinton River crosses downtown, where it was set in concrete in 1963 to prevent flooding.

Settlers came in 1818 and the settlement became the Oakland County seat two years later. Village status followed in 1837 and city status in 1861. Carriage makers turned into auto-body builders, and General Motors assembly plants drew tens of thousands of workers in the 1910s and 1920s. The older housing near downtown, including the Fairgrove Avenue Historic District, dates from that period.

The Silverdome opened in 1975 and hosted Detroit Lions football for years. Population has fallen since 1980 as auto jobs shrank, and the state ran city finances through an emergency manager from 2009 through 2013. Current values are in the next section.

How do Pontiac's housing statistics read today?

Federal survey data for 2020 to 2024 shows the middle owner-occupied value at $121,700 and the middle rent at $1,063. Owners occupy 46.6% of the housing, a smaller share than in Novi, Oak Park or Port Huron, so a large part of the stock is rented.

  • Adults 25 and over holding a bachelor's degree: 16.1%.
  • Average commute: 21.2 minutes.

Woodward Avenue (M-1) runs through town and loops around downtown, Huron Street is M-59, and Telegraph Road is US 24. I-75 and its business loop pass through. Amtrak's Wolverine connects Pontiac with Chicago through Detroit, three trips each way daily. The School District of the City of Pontiac runs Pontiac High School. Four charter schools operate in the city: Pontiac Academy for Excellence, Arts and Technology Academy, Walton Charter and Great Lakes Academy. Notre Dame Preparatory, a private Catholic high school, is in the northeast part. Buyers ask which one serves the address, so confirm with the district before you list.

Do zoning and historic-district rules touch a Pontiac sale?

They can. The city's planning forms include Zoning Board of Appeals applications, a Historic District Approval application and a Zoning Compliance application. A house in the Fairgrove Avenue district or another historic area may need approval for exterior changes, so a buyer planning work will ask what is allowed.

Curb cuts and driveways on state roads such as Woodward and Telegraph need a permit from the State of Michigan, not the city. If your lot touches one of them and you changed the driveway, keep the paperwork. Oakland County's Water Resources Commission runs soil erosion control inside Pontiac, which matters for a vacant lot or a house with grading work underway. For anything else, ask Pontiac planning staff what applies to the parcel.

Does Pontiac regulate rental houses that are being sold?

Yes. The city code requires owners of one- and two-family dwellings occupied by someone other than the owner to register them with the Department of Building Safety. A new owner re-registers within 60 days after a change of ownership, and late registration draws a $25.00 fee per rental unit per month.

  • Registered dwellings are inspected at intervals of no more than three years.
  • A vacated unit needs an inspection before anyone moves back in, and the owner must tell Building Safety first.
  • Occupying a unit before a certificate of compliance is issued is a municipal civil infraction carrying a $500.00 fine, with each day a separate offense.
  • A property whose recorded land contract names the occupant is exempt from the registry.

If you own a tenant-occupied house in the city, ask Building Safety for the certificate status before you sell. A buyer who plans to rent it will have to register within 60 days.

What does the Oakland County deed office handle for a Pontiac sale?

Recording belongs to the county, not the city. Staff examine each document and record those that meet statutory requirements.

Transfer tax applies when the consideration exceeds $99.99, and warranty deeds need a treasurer's tax certificate. The same office collects redemption payments on Sheriff Deed and Clerk Deed foreclosures, open only to people with an interest in the property, so an owner facing a foreclosure sale should ask about the payoff amount before picking a buyer.

Recorded documents can be copied through the county, and its index reaches back to January 1, 1964. If you inherited the house, pull the recorded chain of title early so a missing document does not hold up closing.

The city lists a Request for Income Tax Compliance Clearance among its income tax forms. Ask the Pontiac income tax office whether that clearance applies to your sale.

Can a Pontiac house with tenants be sold?

Yes, but registration and inspection rules apply. Pontiac requires one- and two-family rentals to be registered with Building Safety and inspected at least every three years, and a buyer must re-register within 60 days of the ownership change.

What is the penalty for occupying a Pontiac rental before inspection?

The ordinance sets a $500.00 municipal civil infraction fine, and each day is a separate offense. The owner or agent must notify Building Safety before a vacated unit is reoccupied.

Which office files a deed for a Pontiac property?

The Oakland County Register of Deeds. A warranty deed needs a treasurer's tax certificate at a $5.00 fee first, and a deed recording costs $30.00.

Does heavy snow matter when selling in Pontiac?

Pontiac averages 36.0 inches of snow a year. Roof condition, gutters and a working furnace matter most, and an empty house needs steady heat so pipes do not freeze before the buyer's inspection.

The Census Bureau reports $121,700 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 to 2024. That is a citywide figure, so compare recent sales on your own block before accepting an offer.

How can a Taylor homeowner sell without a long wait?

A Taylor owner may hire an agent, locate a buyer privately, or accept cash from someone willing to take the house as it stands. The house itself often decides, since Downriver neighborhoods like Taylor hold many older, modestly priced homes where repair bills can exceed what owners expected.

Taylor's median home value is $152,600 in Census figures, and 18.4% of residents live in poverty. An owner whose roof or furnace has failed may have no savings left to fix it first, and a direct purchase of the house as is becomes worth a look.

  • Agent listing: strongest price potential when the house shows well and a financed buyer can be waited out.
  • Do it yourself: saves the commission, yet you still need a purchase agreement, title work and a recorded deed.
  • Cash sale: no repairs or open houses, with the closing date negotiated in the contract.

One Taylor rule affects every route: the city wants a certificate of occupancy whenever ownership changes, as explained below.

What is Taylor like, and where does it sit?

Taylor spans about 23.6 square miles of Wayne County, and the 2025 Census estimate is 61,279 people. Dearborn Heights is its northern neighbor, and Allen Park and Southgate touch its eastern line. I-94 passes through the north end, I-75 clips the southeast, and Telegraph Road (US 24) serves as the main spine.

Peter Coan bought the first parcel from the federal government in 1830, and residents carved out Taylor Township in 1847, naming it for Zachary Taylor. A railroad stop built in 1876 became known as Hand Corners. Voters chose cityhood in November 1966, and the charter won approval on March 6, 1968. Southland Shopping Center arrived in 1970 at Eureka and Pardee roads, and Trader's Pointe opened in June 2018 on the old Gibraltar Trade Center site.

Heritage Park, with Coan Lake, a near replica of the old train station and the relocated 1882 West Mound church building, is a local draw. The Downriver campus of Wayne County Community College District is on Northline Road.

Which Census figures matter to Taylor sellers?

Buyer budgets drive this market. Two of every three homes have owner occupants, and the typical value trails Sterling Heights, Troy and Walker by a wide margin.

Does Taylor require a certificate of occupancy when a house is sold?

Yes. Under Zoning Ordinance Section 25.06, the Building Department says, ownership changes call for a certificate of occupancy before anyone moves in. One certificate covers a single owner's time holding the house and does not pass to the next buyer.

This matters when you accept a fast offer. If the buyer cannot move in until the city issues the certificate, a repair item raised in the inspection can hold up occupancy. Ask the Building Department at 734-287-6550 what an inspector will check, and whether anything on the house could fail. The department is at 23555 Goddard Road, and its building inspectors keep short office hours each weekday morning and late afternoon.

Exterior work such as fences, siding, windows, roofing and concrete needs a permit, as does interior work that changes structure. Painting, tile and carpet do not. The city says no work can start until a permit has been issued, so pull permits for any repair you make before closing.

What should a Taylor seller line up in the first week?

Begin with a few calls and one printout. A short list keeps a quick sale moving.

  • Print the current tax bill from the city's online tax lookup, which shows the balance and any penalty.
  • Call the Building Department at 734-287-6550 about the certificate of occupancy and any open permits.
  • Request a lender payoff letter when a mortgage remains.
  • Collect the lease and rental certificate if tenants live in the house.
  • Choose whether a title company or an attorney will prepare the deed for the Wayne County Register of Deeds.

Each task is small, and together they head off most surprises in a buyer's title search.

What do rented houses in Taylor need before a sale?

Rental houses carry their own paperwork. City code Article V, Sections 8-100 through 8-111, calls for registration and a rental certificate of compliance, which stays valid three years and must be renewed before it lapses. Fines run $150 for a first violation, $250 for a second and $500 afterward, and each day can count separately.

Give a buyer both the lease and the current certificate. A new owner inherits the same duties, so a missing certificate becomes that owner's first expense.

What stands out about Taylor's economy and schools?

Shopping is a visible part of the local economy. The Census Bureau reports $1.71 billion in retail sales for 2022, or $27,683 per resident, and the Eureka Road corridor around Southland Shopping Center holds a large part of it. Masco, founded in Taylor in 1929, moved its headquarters out around 2015, and its former property was leased by Ford. Heritage Hospital and the Wayne County Community College District's Downriver campus add jobs and students.

The Taylor School District has a single comprehensive high school, Taylor High on Beech Daly Road. Charter options include Taylor Preparatory High School, Taylor Exemplar Academy and Trillium Academy. Municipal buildings cluster along Goddard Road near Telegraph, and Northline Road leads to the college and the south entrance of Heritage Park.

Other Census items worth knowing: 19.2% of residents are Black, 7.6% are Hispanic or Latino, 12.1% of people under 65 have a disability, and 2,922 residents are veterans.

What transfer tax and recording costs come with a Taylor sale?

Wayne County states its levies on the register's page: county $0.55 and state $3.75, each per $500 of the price. The grantor pays them when the deed is recorded, and MCL 207.523 names the seller as liable. A deed qualifying for an exemption skips the tax, provided it cites the lettered subsection of MCL 207.526 or MCL 207.505.

Recording itself costs $30.00 per document since January 1, 2026: a $26.00 fee and a $4.00 state survey and remonumentation charge. Warranty deeds need a Wayne County Treasurer tax certification beforehand. The recording desk answers at (313) 224-5851, and the office suggests having an attorney prepare the deed.

How do Taylor tax bills work around a closing?

The summer bill is due September 30, and the winter bill falls due in mid-February. A real property balance still open on March 1 goes to the Wayne County Treasurer, and a second unpaid year exposes the house to tax foreclosure. Taylor cuts the summer bill along a July 1 to June 30 year and the winter bill along December 1 to November 30, so closing proration follows those periods.

Homeowners 62 or older whose income stayed below $40,000 can defer the summer bill by applying before September 30. Delinquent water charges and unpaid ordinance citations may be added to a bill as special assessments. Michigan Treasury says taxable value uncaps in the calendar year after a transfer, so a buyer should plan for a larger bill. The assessor's number is 734-374-1315.

Is an inspection part of selling in Taylor?

What is the Wayne County cost to record a deed?

A flat $30.00 per document, effective January 1, 2026. Transfer tax comes on top unless the deed is exempt.

Does the buyer or the seller owe Taylor transfer tax?

The statute puts it on the seller. A purchase agreement can assign it to the buyer by agreement.

What if taxes are late when I sell my Taylor house?

After March 1 the balance sits with the county treasurer, and the title agent deducts what is owed from your proceeds at closing.

Are rented houses treated differently in Taylor?

Yes. They need registration and a three-year certificate of compliance, with fines starting at $150 for a violation.

How can a Dearborn Heights owner sell quickly or at full price?

Options include an agent listing, a sale you arrange yourself with a buyer you found, and an as-is purchase by an investor paying cash. Whichever you pick, the register of deeds office for Wayne County records the deed, transfer tax is paid at recording, and the city asks sellers to complete a few steps of its own.

A well-kept house can sell through a normal listing. Deferred repairs, a deceased owner's estate or a tenant dispute often point toward a cash sale, since the buyer absorbs the condition and the closing timeline is shorter.

  • Listing: the biggest buyer pool, plus inspection and financing contingencies.
  • Direct sale: fewer fees, with more paperwork landing on you.
  • Investor purchase: as-is, a quicker close and a price that reflects repairs.

What shapes a Dearborn Heights sale geographically?

Dearborn Heights is an inner-ring suburb about 12 miles west of downtown Detroit, packed into under 12 square miles. It was created in 1960 from two separate sections of Dearborn Township joined by a quarter-mile strip of Inkster, which explains its unusual shape. The city counted 63,292 residents in 2020, up 9.6% from the 2010 count.

Water shapes parts of the city. The southern portion lies in the Ecorse Creek watershed, where the area around the creek is subject to flooding, and the north drains toward the Rouge River. The Building Department posts a flood zone map, so check your parcel before you price the house.

A city official put Arab residents at about 25% of the population in 2014, and the Census figures below show how common another home language is. Marketing in more than one language can widen your buyer pool.

How do Dearborn Heights housing figures stack up?

Dearborn Heights has a median home value above $185,000 and an average household of 2.76 people. Figures from the Census Bureau follow.

Which school districts serve Dearborn Heights houses?

The city is split among five public districts, which makes the exact address matter. North-end residents are usually in Crestwood School District or Dearborn Public Schools, and south-end residents in Westwood Community Schools or the Dearborn Heights School District No. 7. A small part falls within Wayne-Westland Community Schools and Taylor School District.

  • Crestwood High School is on Beech Daly Road.
  • Hamilton Robichaud High School is on Janet Street in Westwood Community Schools.
  • Annapolis High School is on Clippert Street in District No. 7.
  • Dearborn Public Schools residents are zoned to River Oaks, Haigh or Lindberg elementary schools.

Put the district in your listing, since buyers who search by school filter on it. The city also has two Catholic K-8 schools, St. Anselm and St. Linus, and charter schools including Clara B. Ford Academy.

Who ends up buying a Dearborn Heights house?

The 2020 census counted 22,904 households in the city, and about a third of them had children under 18 living at home. The median age was 35.7, with a quarter of residents under 18, a pattern that favors family buyers who care about bedrooms, yards and school zones. Of 24,076 housing units, only 4.9% stood vacant, and the homeowner vacancy rate was 1.4%.

Local amenities can help a listing. The Dearborn Heights Library System runs two branches, the Caroline Kennedy Library and the John F. Kennedy Jr. Library, and a Henry Ford College campus operated in the north end from the mid-1970s until 2014.

Buyers tend to ask about three items: the flood history of the lot, how old the roof and furnace are, and the school district. Have answers ready for each, since a clear, documented house negotiates better than one with open questions.

What does the city ask Dearborn Heights sellers to do?

The city's own page for buyers and sellers sets out a short list. If the house is your primary residence, you must rescind the Principal Residence Exemption when it sells. The title company may hand you the Request to Rescind at closing, and if not, the Assessor's Office at 313-791-3460 can give it to you. This applies even to a quit claim deed with no title company involved.

The same page tells sellers to contact the Building Department at 6045 Fenton (313-791-3470) to learn which inspections the sale requires, since the city offers a residential certificate inspection application. It also tells sellers to contact the Water Department for a final meter reading.

On the buyer's side, the Property Transfer Affidavit has to reach the assessor inside 45 days of the deed. A late filing can cost up to $200 on a primary residence, and as much as $4,000 on other residential property.

What will the Wayne County recording desk charge?

The county's recording fee rose on January 1, 2026, the first change since 1996. A deed now costs $26, plus the $4 state survey and remonumentation fee, for $30 on each document, however long it is.

At the counter, tax is taken the moment the deed is handed in, and the office wants cash, a check or a money order made payable to it. Tax is 55 cents per $500 for the county plus $3.75 per $500 for the state, which works out to $8.60 per $1,000. A sale at $185,000 therefore owes $1,591.

A warranty deed needs the Wayne County Treasurer's certification that taxes are paid before it can be recorded. Every deed has to name the price or cite the exemption statute, and it needs original signatures and a notary acknowledgment. Calling the Register of Deeds at (313) 224-5851 before submission can prevent a rejection.

When does an investor purchase beat a listing here?

It fits when the house has problems a retail buyer would refuse, when a deadline looms, or when you would rather skip showings. Typical cases are a house needing mechanical work, an inherited property, a landlord ready to exit, and a home with open city inspection items.

Before accepting, get the offer on paper, find out who pays recording and title costs, and make sure the buyer will cooperate with the city's rescind and inspection steps. A second quote costs little and shows whether the first is reasonable. Ask also how the buyer handles the Wayne County Treasurer's tax certification, since recording stalls without it.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate inspection required to sell in Dearborn Heights?

The city directs sellers to its Building Department to find out which inspections apply, and it offers a residential certificate inspection application. Call 313-791-3470 before you list so you know what is required for your address.

Which taxes hit the seller at Dearborn Heights closing?

Add the county's 55 cents and the state's $3.75 on each $500 of price and you get $8.60 per $1,000, so $200,000 means $1,720, collected as the deed is recorded.

Who files the Property Transfer Affidavit?

The buyer sends it to the Assessor's Office, and it is due 45 calendar days after the deed is signed. A late filing can carry a fine, so the seller should remind the buyer at closing.

What if I buy my next home before this one sells?

Michigan allows only one principal residence exemption, so you must rescind the Dearborn Heights exemption once you move out. The new city may ask for a stamped copy of the rescind form before it grants an exemption on the new home.

Is a flood-prone Dearborn Heights house sellable?

Yes. Parts of the south end sit in the Ecorse Creek watershed where flooding occurs, so check the city's flood zone map and tell your buyer what you know about water in the basement.

How does the lake affect selling a house in St. Clair Shores?

Lake St. Clair touches nearly every part of a St. Clair Shores sale, from canal and lakefront houses to the flood-zone check that follows insurance quotes. Water covers close to 19 percent of the city, and part of the city lies in the FEMA floodplain, so learn your own address's status early.

The city sits in southern Macomb County on the lake's western shore, about 14 miles northeast of downtown Detroit, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 57,872 residents. Three selling routes are common:

  • A listing with an agent fits a well-kept house and an owner willing to wait out a buyer's loan.
  • A sale by owner saves the commission and leaves contracts and title steps to you.
  • A cash sale as-is suits deferred repairs, tenants or an estate. Compare offers and note who covers which closing costs.

What is St. Clair Shores like for a seller?

The city measures 14.40 square miles overall, with 2.72 of them water. About 14 miles of canals, most along the Nautical Mile, the Jefferson Avenue strip between 9 Mile and 10 Mile Roads that holds restaurants, boat dealers and marinas. The 28-story Shore Club Sky Tower, at the foot of Nine Mile Road, is the tallest structure in town.

French settlers arrived as early as 1710, and farms dominated until the early 1900s. The village formed in 1925, and residents chose cityhood in January 1951. Many subdivisions were platted early but built out only after World War II, making this Detroit's fastest-growing suburb in the 1950s. Jefferson Beach Amusement Park ran on the lakefront from 1927 to 1959.

Youth hockey is a local tradition, with two municipal ice arenas at the civic recreation center. Interstate 94 skirts the western edge through exits 224 to 230, about 13 miles from midtown Detroit.

Population peaked decades ago. The census counted 63,096 residents in 2000, 59,715 in 2010 and 58,874 in 2020, while land density eased from 5,139.5 to 5,040.2 people per square mile between 2010 and 2020. During Prohibition the lakefront village was known for roadhouses and rum running, and the Miss St. Clair Shores scholarship program has run since 1953.

Neighbors matter when you describe a location. Roseville and Eastpointe lie to the west, and Harper Woods, Grosse Pointe Woods and Grosse Pointe Shores lie to the south across the Wayne County line. The area was part of Erin Township from 1843 to 1911 and then of Lake Township, so older records for the city may carry those names. Ask the title company to search under them if a document looks incomplete.

How does the floodplain affect a St. Clair Shores sale?

The city's flood page explains that FEMA redraws its maps now and then, so a parcel once in the floodplain may now be outside it, and the reverse can happen. Buyers often ask about flood status, since insurers and lenders look at it.

The city names two lookup tools:

  • Macomb County GIS: type the address, open Layers, expand Natural Features and tick Flood Zones. A parcel that turns red may be in the zone.
  • FEMA's flood map search by street address.

If an insurer has placed the house in the floodplain and you hold a survey or other evidence against it, you may qualify for a Letter of Map Amendment, or you can use the city's Options to Appeal Determination form. Sorting this out before listing spares you a surprise during a buyer's loan review.

Which school districts and roads do buyers ask about?

Three public districts share the city. South Lake Schools covers the south, Lakeview Public Schools the middle and Lake Shore Public Schools the north, and each runs a high school inside the city limits. Ask the districts to confirm a specific address, because buyers want that detail.

Private options include St. Isaac Jogues and St. Joan of Arc, while St. Germaine closed in 2024. Wikipedia credits the city's popularity to its lakefront, park system, recreation programs and choice of districts.

I-94 and Jefferson Avenue carry most commuters. Census puts the average trip to work at 26.7 minutes, the longest among these four cities.

What do St. Clair Shores rules say about rental houses?

The city wants every non-owner-occupied house registered and holding a certificate of approval before anyone moves in. Its registration form prints these terms:

  • Single-family house: $150 for the first 3,000 square feet, then $10 for each added 1,000 square feet.
  • Multiple-family building: $150 for the first unit, then $50 for each added unit in that building.
  • The fee pays for the first inspection and one follow-up. A rescheduled visit when nobody is on site costs $30, and a failed-compliance reinspection costs half the original fee.
  • An owner who lives beyond Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Washtenaw and St. Clair counties must name a local agent.
  • Once the house sells, send the city a recorded deed or land contract to be dropped from its records.

Community Development and Inspections, at 586-447-3340, can confirm what applies to your address and whether an open permit needs closing before a sale.

What will the Macomb County recorder charge me?

The Register of Deeds in Mount Clemens, on N. Main Street, records deeds for a $30 fee however many pages they run. Of that amount, $4 supports the state survey and remonumentation fund. Call (586) 469-7953 with questions.

A tax certificate from the County Treasurer must come first for warranty deeds and land contracts, along with their covenant-clause and assignment variants. The fee page lists it at $5 for up to five legal descriptions.

The county's transfer tax table multiplies the sale price by 0.0075 for the state and by 0.0011 for the county. Your title company can turn those rates into a dollar total at your price.

Treasury's ownership FAQ adds that the buyer reports the change of ownership to the assessor on Form 2766 inside 45 days.

Check Macomb County GIS or FEMA's flood map search, both linked by the city. Part of the city is in the FEMA floodplain, and a survey that shows otherwise may support a Letter of Map Amendment.

What do recording and transfer tax cost on a Macomb sale?

Recording is $30 per document. The county schedule lists state transfer tax at 0.0075 of the sale price and county tax at 0.0011.

Do rental houses have to be registered in St. Clair Shores?

Yes. Registration and a certificate of approval come before occupancy, and a single-family house starts at $150 for the first 3,000 square feet.

Which school district serves my street?

South Lake Schools serves the south, Lakeview Public Schools the middle and Lake Shore Public Schools the north. Confirm your address with the district.

How big is the city?

14.40 square miles in total, with 2.72 of water, while the Census Bureau lists 11.68 square miles of land. The 2020 census counted 58,874 residents.

Selling in Royal Oak?

What sets a Royal Oak house sale apart?

Sellers here deal with the city's Assessing and Building divisions and the Oakland County Register of Deeds, and one variable is whether the house is a registered rental. An owner-occupied house needs the deed, the transfer affidavits and the tax steps, while a rental adds city registration and inspection rules.

This Oakland County suburb lies roughly 10 miles north of downtown Detroit on the Woodward Corridor, with I-75 and I-696 close by. A survey party named it in 1819 for a large oak tree, and it incorporated as a village in 1891 and again as a city in 1921. Royal Oak calls itself the city of trees, and the National Arbor Day Foundation has recognized it as a Tree City USA every year since 1976.

What draws buyers to Royal Oak?

The downtown is among the largest in the Detroit suburbs, and buyers notice how close a house sits to it. Since the late 1990s the blocks along Main Street and Washington Avenue have turned into a dining and entertainment district, with condominium and loft buildings adding residents.

  • Most of the Detroit Zoo lies in Royal Oak, with a portion reaching into Huntington Woods.
  • Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital is among the city's listed points of interest.
  • The Royal Oak Music Theatre, the Baldwin Theatre and a comedy club bring evening crowds.
  • Arts, Beats and Eats fills downtown over Labor Day weekend, and the city sponsors events around the Woodward Dream Cruise.
  • The Farmers Market began in 1925 and now stands at 11 Mile Road and Troy Street.

Buyers touring houses near downtown tend to ask about noise, parking and event traffic, so describe event weekends honestly.

Where did Royal Oak's trees and the Red Run come from?

The city grew up around a small river, the Red Run. During the 1930s a WPA project filled in the stretch beside Vinsetta Boulevard, which had been built with the stream as its median, and in 1967 and 1968 the rest of the river inside Oakland County was buried in a six-foot drain pipe. Extensive tree planting since the 1930s earned Royal Oak its nickname, though recent development has sparked arguments over how the urban forest is maintained.

For a seller, the practical point is the mature canopy. Older streets with large trees are part of what buyers picture when they search here, so photograph the yard in full leaf.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Royal Oak house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What is the housing picture in Royal Oak?

Per capita income reaches $66,293 and household income $101,109 at the midpoint. Federal figures for 2020 to 2024 put the middle owner-occupied home at $328,700, owners in 68.0 percent of homes and rent at $1,381.

Households are small. The average has 1.98 people, 42.3 percent of 2020 households were one person, and only 14.8 percent of residents are minors. Some 82.8 percent kept the same address for a year, and 64.1 percent of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree or more.

An estimated 57,583 people lived here in July 2025, 1.1 percent fewer than the 2020 base. The 1970 count of 86,238 was the peak, and numbers have hovered near 57,000 to 58,000 since 2010. On 11.79 square miles that is about 4,937 people per square mile, so a listing competes with many similar blocks and presentation matters.

Which public school districts cover Royal Oak?

Royal Oak Schools teach most children, though a portion of the city's land is zoned to Berkley Public Schools, so confirm your address before listing. Enrollment decline led the district to merge its two high schools, Dondero and Kimball, into Royal Oak High School in 2006, and its two middle schools into one in 2007.

Private options include schools tied to the Shrine of the Little Flower parish, and a branch of Oakland Community College sits in the city. Families will ask about the district boundary first.

What must a Royal Oak rental owner handle?

Registration with the city comes before any tenant moves in, and the Building Division inspects residential rental units under the Property Maintenance Code. The city's guide tells owners to name a responsible party within 30 miles, post the address inside the unit, respect occupancy limits and keep smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and extinguishers working.

Short-term rentals also need insurance and must hand guests the city's Good Neighbor Policy. A buyer will want to see the registration paperwork, and an unregistered rental is a problem to fix before closing. Penalties escalate with each violation:

Royal Oak rental ordinance penalties by offense, from the city's registration guide
ViolationPenalty
FirstCivil fine of at least $200 plus costs
SecondCivil fine of at least $350 plus costs
ThirdMisdemeanor, fine up to $500, up to 90 days in jail, or both, and registration may be revoked

Questions go to the Building Division at building@romi.gov, and registration fees pay for the inspections.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Royal Oak houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do Royal Oak assessments and tax bills work for a seller?

The summer bill is due July 31 and the winter bill February 14, and postmarks are not accepted as proof of payment. A late summer bill accrues interest of one-half of 1 percent a month from August 1, and anything unpaid on March 1 goes to the Oakland County Treasurer. Owners may split the summer bill into two halves, due July 31 and October 31.

Assessed value sits at 50 percent of true cash value, while taxable value is limited by an inflation multiplier until a transfer. The Assessor's Office reviews the deed and affidavit for every transferred property, which lifts the cap. To estimate a new bill, the city suggests treating half the purchase price as taxable value, dividing by 1,000 and multiplying by the millage rate.

An owner who lived in the home before May 1 of the prior year qualifies for the Principal Residence Exemption, which the city says carries a rate about 15 mills below a non-homestead property. Appeals begin at the March Board of Review, and July and December sessions correct clerical errors and mutual mistakes. Homeowners can read their parcel records free on BS&A Online, so check yours before a buyer does.

What paper rules does the Oakland County recorder enforce?

The county examines each document before recording it, so a defect can cost weeks. Page one needs a 2.5 inch top margin and half-inch margins on every other side, and the deed must be notarized. Deeds signed before April 6, 2017 had to state the marital status of male grantors, and those signed before March 4, 2002 needed two witnesses.

  • A Sidwell Validation Unit approves the legal description before the cashier takes payment.
  • Counter hours are 8:30 am to 4:30 pm on weekdays.
  • Copies are $1 a page, and a certified copy adds $5.

Any instrument with consideration above $99.99 is taxed, and MCL 207.523 puts the bill on the seller. The county's printed shares are $1.10 per $1,000 to the county and $7.50 per $1,000 to the state.

Frequently asked questions

Must a Royal Oak landlord register before selling?

Registration is required before renting, so an occupied rental should already be registered. Hand the buyer the paperwork and ask the Building Division what the new owner files.

What are Royal Oak's tax due dates?

July 31 for the summer bill and February 14 for the winter bill. The summer bill can be split, with the second half due October 31.

How does the homestead exemption change after a sale?

The buyer applies on the new home, and the city says it lowers the rate about 15 mills against non-homestead property. Rescind your own exemption when you sell.

What does the county charge to file a Royal Oak deed?

$30 per deed, with the $4 survey surcharge included. Warranty deeds also need a $5 tax certificate from the treasurer.

Does taxable value reset when I sell in Royal Oak?

Sell My House Fast in Kentwood, MI: Options, Costs and Cash Offers

Cash Home Buyers in Michigan
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentwood, MI: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentwood, MI sale
  • Turn the Kentwood, MI offer down and you owe us nothing

Sell Your Kentwood House for Cash
