Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Kentwood?
We buy Kentwood houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Where does a Kentwood home sale begin?

Kentwood sits in Kent County on the southeast side of Grand Rapids, and a sale there follows Michigan's county recording rules plus a few city offices you will deal with directly. Kentwood's July 2025 population estimate is 54,776, which is 0.8 percent above the 2020 base.

Most sellers meet three questions early: what the house might fetch, what the city requires before title moves, and how the tax bill is split at closing. This page answers each with Kentwood's own figures and offices, so any route you choose starts from local facts.

How is Kentwood laid out, and what does that mean for a home sale?

Kentwood covers about 21 square miles of land and is bordered by Wyoming on the west, Grand Rapids and Grand Rapids Township to the north, Cascade Township to the east and Gaines Township to the south. It was incorporated in 1967 out of Paris Township, partly to stop neighboring cities from annexing more land, and it took its name from the Kentwood Public Schools.

Road access shapes how quickly buyers can reach a house. The main routes are:

  • I-96, which clips the northeast corner of the city
  • M-11 along 28th Street, a busy commercial strip
  • M-37 along East Beltline Avenue and Broadmoor Avenue
  • M-6, the southern bypass linking I-196 near Hudsonville with I-96 near the Gerald R. Ford International Airport

Two paths, the Paul Henry Rail Trail and the East-West Trail, run through town, and homes near them tend to be easy to describe in a listing. School boundaries matter too: Kentwood Public Schools serves most addresses, while Forest Hills Public Schools and Kelloggsville Public Schools cover parts of the city. Confirm the district for your street before pricing.

What do the Census numbers say about Kentwood housing?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures describe a city where owners are the majority and median rent runs $1,260 a month. The table lists the figures that bear most on a sale.

Kentwood housing and household figures, Census QuickFacts
MeasureKentwood
Median value of owner-occupied homes$268,200
Owner-occupied housing rate61.3%
Median gross rent$1,260
Households21,245
Median household income$74,373
Same house one year ago86.2%

About four in ten homes are rented, so many Kentwood sellers are landlords, and the next section covers the rental certificate that affects them. A median value is a midpoint for the whole city. It will not predict your street, so ask for sold comparables from the same school attendance area.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kentwood house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Does winter in Kentwood affect what buyers look for?

Yes, because Kentwood has a warm-summer continental climate with real cold. Mean daily highs in January sit near 30 degrees Fahrenheit and mean lows near 15, and the area gets roughly 34 inches of precipitation across a year, spread fairly evenly from month to month.

Inspectors in town spend their time on the furnace, attic insulation, roof and basement. If one of them is worn out, either repair it before listing or sell as-is at a price that reflects the work. An as-is cash sale hands that repair risk to the buyer. Whatever route you take, get the furnace serviced and keep the receipt, because heating questions come up first in almost every walkthrough.

Does a rental house in Kentwood need a certificate before it changes hands?

A rental dwelling in Kentwood must be registered and hold a valid certificate of compliance, and that certificate stays with the owner who earned it. Under the city's rental dwelling inspection ordinance, a certificate can pass to a buyer only if the sale closes within 90 days of the certificate being issued and the buyer tells the city within 30 days of the sale.

The details that matter to a landlord seller:

  • A six-year certificate does not transfer. If it moves to a new owner inside the 90-day window it reverts to a two-year certificate.
  • Failure by the buyer to notify the city results in suspension of the certificate, and a replacement is dated back to the sale with fees owed from that date.
  • An owner who lives in a condominium unit needs no registration or certification, but a condominium owned as a rental is treated as a single-family rental.
  • Certificates cannot be issued while the property has unpaid city bills.

Call the Inspections Department at 616-554-0700 before you sign a contract on a rental, so the certificate dates and any open violations are known in advance.

When are Kentwood property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Kentwood mails summer bills in the first week of July, due August 20, and winter bills in the first week of December, due February 14. Unpaid balances move to the Kent County Treasurer on March 1, and a qualifying owner has until September 15 to file a summer deferment with the city.

The assessment side runs on a fixed yearly rhythm:

  • Change notices go out soon after February 1 and carry the appeal dates.
  • The Board of Review begins hearings on the Tuesday after the first Monday in March, by appointment.
  • A homeowner still unsatisfied after the board has until July 31 to petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • Occupants claim the school-tax exemption on a homestead by June 1 to cover the summer bill, or November 1 for winter.

Appeals cannot rest on a neighbor's lower tax bill. Michigan lets taxable value rise more slowly for long-term owners, so a recent buyer will usually pay more than an owner next door who has held the house for years.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentwood houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to the tax bill and the exemption after a Kentwood sale?

After the deed records, the buyer owes the Kentwood Assessor a property transfer affidavit within 45 days. Taxable value then resets to the state equalized value for the next tax year, so the buyer's first full bill may look nothing like yours.

As the seller, stop claiming your principal residence exemption by filing the rescission form with the city within 90 days of moving out. Owners who already bought a new Michigan home while the old one sits unsold can ask for a conditional rescission, which Kentwood says may run up to three tax years if the house is never rented. The state form is 4640.

Recording happens downtown in the County Administration Building, 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Two transfer taxes attach to the deed: the state levy of $3.75 per $500 of price, and a county levy that Michigan sets at 55 cents per $500 below 2,000,000 residents. Your title agent should show both on the settlement statement.

Should you list in Kentwood or take an investor's cash offer?

An investor's cash offer usually closes faster and carries fewer conditions, while a listing reaches more buyers but adds showings and lender timelines. Neither is free of cost, so compare net figures.

Before you sign anything, list your own requirements: a closing date, the mortgage payoff and a plan for tenants. Ask each buyer in writing who covers recording costs and whether open city violations stay with the house. The Assessor's online sales search shows qualified Kentwood sales, which helps you judge whether an offer sits near the neighborhood's range.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Census say a Kentwood house is worth?

Census data for 2020 to 2024 gives a median owner-occupied value of $268,200 in Kentwood. It is a citywide midpoint only.

Who collects Kentwood property tax, and where do unpaid taxes go?

Kentwood's summer bill is due August 20 and its winter bill February 14. Whatever is still open on March 1 goes to the county.

What paperwork follows a Kentwood sale?

Mostly the buyer's paperwork: the transfer affidavit goes to the assessor. Your part is the rescission of your principal residence exemption, plus a rental certificate check with Inspections if you were a landlord.

Can I sell a Kentwood rental with tenants still living there?

Yes, but the rental certificate must be valid and the buyer must notify the city within 30 days of the sale for a transferred certificate to stay in force. Call Inspections at 616-554-0700 first.

Which county office records the deed for a Kentwood sale?

The Kent County Register of Deeds, downtown at 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Transfer tax is collected at that recording.

Selling in Battle Creek?
We buy Battle Creek houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which selling route suits a Battle Creek owner?

Owners here usually weigh three paths: an agent listing, a private sale, or a cash investor willing to buy it with all its flaws. Every path finishes at the Calhoun County Register of Deeds with a recorded deed and Michigan transfer tax.

Speed and certainty pull in opposite directions. A listing reaches the most buyers but leans on a lender's appraisal and an inspection report. A cash sale gives up some price for a shorter road, which tends to matter most for a house that is empty, inherited, behind on city code items or full of tenants you would rather not manage.

  • Agent sale: fits a house in decent repair and a seller with months to spare.
  • Private sale: saves the commission, yet pricing, showings and paperwork are yours.
  • Cash purchase: no repair requests, and the closing day is often negotiable.

What makes Battle Creek different from other Michigan cities?

The city sits in northwestern Calhoun County at the junction of the Kalamazoo River and Battle Creek, and at roughly 43 square miles it ranks third among Michigan cities by area. Part of that size dates to the early 1980s, when it annexed Battle Creek Township and nearly doubled in population. A good deal of the acreage is not housing at all, because the Fort Custer industrial park and training grounds occupy a large share.

Cereal built the place. Kellogg's and Post both began in town, and the employer list from the local development agency includes Denso (about 2,500 jobs), WK Kellogg Co (2,000), FireKeepers Casino Hotel, the VA Medical Center, the Hart-Dole-Inouye Federal Center, Bronson Battle Creek and Fort Custer Training Center. Many buyers pick a house by its drive to one of those sites.

I-94 passes through, about midway between Detroit and Chicago, and the Amtrak station shares a building with intercity bus service. Winters are hard on houses: the 1991 to 2020 record averages about 65 inches of snow and 45 snowy days a year, which tests roofs, gutters and furnaces.

How do Battle Creek housing numbers compare with income?

About two of every three households here own their home, and values sit well under Detroit-area prices. These numbers come from the Census Bureau's profile of the city.

Housing and income snapshot for Battle Creek

The 2025 estimate sits 1.4% under the 2020 count of 52,721, which points to a steady market instead of a fast-growing one. Buyers will compare your price with what their monthly payment would be.

What happens to a Battle Creek house once it sits empty?

A vacant-structure ordinance catches many sellers off guard. When the city identifies a house as empty or abandoned, the owner of record gets a registration form with a 30-day response window and a $25 fee, then a $40 monthly monitoring charge invoiced quarterly. Unpaid charges from March and September can be added to the property tax bill.

  • An open house gets an order to secure it within 72 hours, or the city boards it up and bills the owner.
  • The certificate of occupancy is suspended at vacancy and revoked after more than 24 months.
  • An owner-occupied house empty 6 to 24 months needs a Property Maintenance Code inspection, and a safety inspection beyond 24 months.
  • A house headed for rental needs registration and an inspection after 2 months or more of vacancy.

Violations stay with the address. In the city's stated position, a new owner gets no added time to correct problems that predate the transfer, which is a common reason a mortgage buyer backs away from a neglected property and an as-is buyer looks simpler.

Where is a Battle Creek deed recorded and what tax comes with it?

Recording takes place in Marshall. The Calhoun County Clerk and Register of Deeds accepts land documents at the county building, 315 West Green Street, and its staff cannot coach you on completing a deed, so bring in a title agent or a lawyer for that.

Two Michigan transfer taxes fall on the seller. The state charges $3.75 for each $500 of value (MCL 207.525), and a county with fewer than 2,000,000 people adds 55 cents per $500 (MCL 207.504). A $150,000 price therefore costs 300 units times $4.30, or $1,290.

Payment is due at the county treasurer within a fortnight of delivering the deed, a window the statute sets at 15 days. Several transfers are exempt, among them a deed to your child or grandchild, a deed in foreclosure and a deed that fixes a title flaw. Ask the Calhoun County Treasurer whether a tax certification is needed first.

What should you do about taxes and the homestead exemption at closing?

Summer taxes attach as a lien on July 1 and winter taxes on December 1. Statewide the payment dates are September 14 and February 14, though a city charter may choose others, so get the exact dates from the Battle Creek City Treasurer and have the closing office split them between you and the buyer.

If you live in the house, send the assessor a Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption (Form 2602) within three months of moving out. Filing late adds $5 a day until a $200 cap is reached, and the exemption drops off the roll at the end of that calendar year. Closing agents commonly hand out the form but carry no legal liability if they forget.

Your buyer faces a different calculation. Taxable value is capped while an owner stays put, yet after a transfer it can rise to full assessed levels, so the first bill may run higher than yours did.

Which Battle Creek sellers do well with an all-cash buyer?

The match is strongest when the preparation a conventional listing demands costs more than the extra price it might bring. Picture a house with a failing roof or furnace, a property idling and accruing monitoring fees, an inherited home with out-of-town heirs, or a rental with a rough tenant history.

Judge each offer by what you keep. Ask who pays recording and title charges, whether the number moves after a walk-through, and how soon you can close. Get terms in writing and a second quote before you commit.

Frequently asked questions

What is a realistic timeline for selling in Battle Creek?

A cash purchase can close within a couple of weeks when title is clear, whereas a listing takes longer because of showings, financing and an appraisal. Liens, probate and open city violations can stretch either path, so check them first.

Does Battle Creek inspect a house before it changes hands?

The city focuses on vacant houses, rentals and addresses with open violations. Phone Code Compliance and ask whether your address has an open case or a suspended certificate of occupancy, since those are what can hold up a sale.

Who is responsible for the state and county transfer tax?

The seller, by statute, though the purchase contract can shift the cost. At $4.30 per $500, a $120,000 sale carries $1,032, and some family transfers qualify for an exemption.

Can a house with tenants be sold in Battle Creek?

Yes. The lease does not end with the sale, so the buyer normally inherits the tenant unless the tenant agrees to leave. For a rental, confirm that registration and the city inspection are current, since a lapse can complicate things.

How soon must I remove my homestead exemption after a sale?

Form 2602 goes to the city assessor, and the clock is 90 days from the move-out. The exemption comes off on December 31 of that year, and each late day adds $5, capped at $200.

Where does a Portage house sale begin?

Portage sellers deal with three offices: the city for permits and property tax bills, the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds for the deed, and the county treasurer for the tax certificate that has to be on a warranty deed. Listing with an agent or selling straight to a buyer changes none of that. The city's online property records search, updated daily, shows the tax and parcel details a buyer will check first.

Portage sits in Kalamazoo County and is the smaller of the two main cities in the Kalamazoo-Portage metro area. The area was settled in 1830 and Portage became a city in 1963. Several things set it apart from a typical Michigan suburb: two lakes in the southeast corner, a very large pharmaceutical plant, and a tornado in May 2024 that cut across town from one side to the other.

How many people live in Portage, and how do they live?

Portage is a wide city: 32.29 square miles of land hold roughly 1,514 people per square mile. Federal estimates for July 1, 2025 count 49,862 residents, a 2.0 percent gain over the April 2020 base of 48,882.

Few households move in a given year: 86.8 percent of residents had the same address twelve months earlier. College degrees are common too, held by 47.9 percent of adults over 25, so expect buyers to compare listings carefully.

What do Portage buyers ask about the lakes and schools?

Buyers who search Portage often start with the water. Austin Lake lies in the southeast part of the city, named for a settler who arrived from New York in 1833, and West Lake sits right beside it with Portage Road running between the two. Houses on or near the lakes are a separate segment from the subdivisions farther north and west.

School district is the other common question, because the city is split. Most of Portage belongs to Portage Public Schools, while smaller areas fall in Comstock Public Schools, Vicksburg Community Schools and Schoolcraft Community Schools. Name the district in your listing, because a parcel's district follows the district boundary and the city on the mailing address says nothing about it.

Average travel to work is 19.7 minutes, and two large employers anchor the local job market:

  • Pfizer runs its largest manufacturing facility in Portage, on about 1,300 acres.
  • Stryker has been headquartered in Portage since 2023 and operates several manufacturing sites in the city.
  • Kalamazoo, the larger of the two main cities in the metro area, supplies much of the rest of the job base.

What did the May 2024 tornado change for Portage sellers?

The tornado that struck Portage on May 7, 2024 was rated high-end EF2, and reports after the storm counted more than 500 damaged buildings, 60 of them destroyed. The city set up a tornado recovery page for residents and businesses, and the damage path is still the first thing some out-of-town buyers ask about.

Did the storm touch your house? Gather the permits, contractor invoices and insurance paperwork into one folder, because even a buyer paying cash wants to know which roof, siding or windows are new. For a house still awaiting repairs, say so early and weigh selling without repairs against paying for a rebuild. Permits for construction work go through the Portage Department of Community Development, and the Treasury Office collects the permit fees.

The city's recovery page also lists nonprofit disaster case management for people affected by the storm, which can help with insurance and housing questions while you decide whether to sell. Ask the city manager's office for current contacts, since program details change over time.

What fees does the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds charge?

Recording one deed in Kalamazoo County costs a flat $30.00, with another $3.00 for each additional instrument a document assigns or discharges. Payment can be cash, check, money order, debit or credit card.

Before recording, a warranty deed, a deed with a covenant of warranty, a land contract or a master deed must carry the county treasurer's tax certificate. It runs $5.00 for up to 20 tax ID numbers and $0.20 for every description beyond that. A separate $10.00 city certificate applies only to parcels inside the City of Kalamazoo, which excludes Portage.

Transfer tax is figured on the price stated in the deed, rounded up to the next $500 step. The county's fee page prints $1.10 per thousand dollars for the county share and $7.50 per thousand dollars for the state share. Michigan's transfer tax act (MCL 207.523) makes the grantor liable, so put that line in your net proceeds estimate and get the exact figure from the title company.

How does the Portage tax calendar affect a seller?

The city collects in two installments. Summer bills open August 1 and are due September 14, and winter bills open December 1 and are due February 14. Each bill covers the full January 1 to December 31 tax year, and a deadline on a weekend rolls to Monday.

  • Balances still open on March 1 pass to the Kalamazoo County Treasury, which adds its own interest and penalties.
  • Special assessments for water, sewer and city street work are billed in July with an August 31 due date, so check for an open installment on the parcel.
  • A lender or escrow agent can request a tax listing from the city after the first bills go out.

For a rough view of the buyer's bill, the city points to the State of Michigan Property Tax Estimator, where future owners enter the state equalized value and current owners enter the taxable value. The Portage assessor's office also has a property record form that corrects square footage, bedroom counts and similar facts. Fix any errors before a buyer's appraiser pulls the record.

What if tenants live in the Portage house?

A tenant can stay through closing or move out first, and the lease together with your notice rights sets the timing.

Since late 2025 the city has also run a rental listing website for landlords, with free listings for owners of fewer than 20 units. A buyer who plans to keep renting may take over the lease as written, which saves you the search for a new tenant. Ask the city's Community Development office which local rules apply to your rental, and bring the current lease to every showing.

Frequently asked questions

What will recording a Portage deed cost?

A flat $30.00 for the deed at the Kalamazoo County Register of Deeds. A warranty deed also needs a treasurer tax certificate at $5.00, which covers up to 20 tax ID numbers.

Does the buyer or the seller owe transfer tax in Portage?

The seller owes it. The statute names the grantor, and the county fee page lists $1.10 and $7.50 per thousand dollars for the two shares.

What are the Portage tax deadlines?

September 14 for the summer bill and February 14 for the winter bill. Weekend dates roll to Monday, and open balances pass to the county on March 1.

Can I sell a Portage house damaged in the 2024 tornado?

Yes. Reports counted over 500 damaged buildings after May 7, 2024, and an unrepaired house sells at a price that reflects the work. Keep permits and insurance records for any repairs.

Which district teaches children from my Portage address?

Usually Portage Public Schools, though some parcels belong to Comstock, Vicksburg or Schoolcraft. Confirm with the district before you print it in a listing.

What makes selling a house in East Lansing different?

East Lansing is a college town built around Michigan State University, and its rental rules decide who can buy and use your house. The city requires a rental license for most non-owner-occupied homes, some neighborhoods bar new rentals, and many single-family houses carry deed restrictions against renting at all. Those facts change which buyers can pay full price.

The city sits in Ingham and Clinton counties, immediately east of Lansing. It was settled in 1847 and incorporated in 1907. The legislature approved a charter proposed under the name College Park but changed the name to East Lansing. MSU was founded in 1855 and moved onto what is now campus ground in 1857, and the city's first seven mayors were professors or college employees. East Lansing stayed a dry city until voters changed the charter in 1968.

Grand River Avenue, a boulevard that grew out of the old Lansing and Howell plank road, runs through downtown and separates the campus from the rest of the city together with Michigan Avenue.

How does East Lansing compare with nearby Michigan cities?

East Lansing has the priciest owned homes of the four cities profiled in this batch of pages and the smallest share of owner-occupants. It is also young, with a median age of 21.8 at the 2020 census, so houses change hands and tenants more often than in a suburb like Eastpointe.

Only 59.5 percent of residents had the same address a year earlier, against 92.3 percent in Eastpointe. With that much movement, an East Lansing listing often meets buyers who plan to rent it out or buy a first home near campus.

What rental rules affect the value of an East Lansing house?

If your buyer plans to rent the house, the license rules matter as much as the price. The city code lists exceptions where no license is needed, and a seller can help a buyer by knowing them.

  • Family of the owner may live in the house without a license, and two unrelated people count as a family.
  • An owner who is away temporarily may use a house-sitting form for up to two years in a five-year period, but a house that is for sale does not qualify.
  • A seller of a house or duplex may stay up to 90 days after closing under a rental agreement without a license.
  • An estate representative may occupy a house for up to two years from the owner's date of death if the owner lived there for the last year.

Putting a house in an LLC removes the owner-occupancy exception, because an LLC has no family members. A new rental license is not automatic. Some areas have a zoning overlay that prohibits new licenses or limits them to owner-occupied homes, and the city's own guidance says a new application takes a minimum of two months and more often three to four. A tenant cannot move in before the license is granted.

Which neighborhoods, schools and roads do East Lansing buyers ask about?

The city lists more than 25 neighborhoods, and many have associations that speak at council and commission meetings. One section is a designated Historic District, and landmark structures in older areas fall under the Historic Preservation Code. Several single-family neighborhoods within a mile of campus have used a petition process under a 2004 zoning ordinance to restrict or prohibit renting.

East Lansing Public Schools reaches most addresses and enrolls just over 3,400 students in six elementary schools, MacDonald Middle School and East Lansing High School. Portions of the city fall in the Lansing, Okemos, Haslett and Bath districts, so confirm the district on the deed address. About one fifth of the East Lansing district's students come from outside the city through Schools of Choice.

Getting around is straightforward, and the Census puts mean commute time at 16.2 minutes, the shortest in this four-city group.

  • Interstates 96, 69 and 496 and US 127 serve the area.
  • CATA buses connect the city with Lansing.
  • Amtrak runs the Blue Water service to Chicago from the Capital Area Multimodal Gateway on South Harrison Road.

How do East Lansing property taxes work at closing?

The city treasury bills both seasons. Summer taxes are levied July 1 and payable without penalty through August 31. Winter taxes are levied December 1 and payable without penalty through February 14 of the following year. Weekend and holiday due dates slide to the next business day, and late payments pick up a 3 percent penalty.

On March 1 each year the city sends unpaid real property taxes to the county, with added interest and penalty. For a payoff after that date, call the Ingham County Treasurer at (517) 676-7220 or the Clinton County Treasurer at (989) 224-5280, depending on where the parcel sits. The city's property tax office, at 410 Abbot Road, takes calls at (517) 319-6826.

Because the city spans two counties, the register of deeds and the county treasurer that apply to you depend on the parcel. Ask the East Lansing assessor which county holds your records before you order a title commitment.

What state costs apply when an East Lansing house sells?

East Lansing sellers owe Michigan's transfer tax, which is $3.75 on each $500 block at the state level (MCL 207.525) with a county layer added (MCL 207.504). Ask the deed office in Ingham or Clinton County for the current county rate. The county treasurer collects it, and the clock is 15 days from handing over the deed.

MCL 207.526 also exempts a quitclaim deed that fixes a flaw in title and an instrument that straightens a boundary line without payment. After closing, the buyer tells the assessor of the transfer within 45 days, and taxable value is reset the following year (MCL 211.27a). Ask the assessor how to rescind your principal residence exemption so the new owner's bill is correct.

What should an East Lansing owner compare before choosing a sale route?

A listing aimed at students and landlords depends on the rental license history of the house, so gather license paperwork and any deed restriction notices first. An owner-occupant buyer cares about school district lines and neighborhood overlay rules instead. A direct sale to an investor can work for a house that needs repairs or has a lapsed license, as long as the contract states who handles the license process.

Frequently asked questions

Is a rental license part of selling my East Lansing house?

No. Licensing applies to renting, so selling does not need one. A seller of a house or duplex may even stay up to 90 days after closing under a rental agreement without a license, which can help when you need time to move.

Will the next owner of my East Lansing house be allowed to rent it?

Maybe. Many single-family houses carry deed restrictions against renting, some neighborhoods have zoning overlays that bar new licenses, and a license application takes a minimum of two months. Buyers should call the city's Planning, Building and Housing department before closing.

What are the East Lansing tax deadlines?

The summer bill is penalty-free through August 31 and the winter bill through February 14. After those dates a 3 percent charge applies, and real property taxes still unpaid on March 1 are sent to the county.

Which county records my East Lansing deed?

The city spans Ingham and Clinton counties. Deed recording and any delinquent tax payoff go through the county that holds your parcel, so confirm with the city assessor before ordering title work.

Who covers the deed tax at an East Lansing closing?

The seller. The state charges $3.75 on each $500 block and the county adds its own rate. Unless the transfer matches a listed exemption, the county treasurer expects payment within 15 days after the deed changes hands.

What do Roseville sellers deal with first?

Roseville is a compact, densely built Macomb County city. Its clearest local rule for sellers covers rental houses, which carry a city Certificate of Compliance and an ownership transfer fee. Every sale, rental or not, also runs through the Macomb County Register of Deeds and the city assessor.

Downtown Detroit lies 13 to 14 miles southwest. Roseville became a village in 1926 and a city in 1958, when the village joined the remainder of Erin Township. A population that tripled between 1950 and 1960 suggests that much of the housing stock dates from that era, so a walk-through before listing shows you what an inspector is likely to flag.

What is the history behind Roseville's streets and shopping centers?

The first permanent post office opened in 1840 and gave the place its name. In 1919 Michigan's first commercial airport, Packard Field, opened at Gratiot Avenue and Frazho Road, and the site later became the Eastgate Shopping Center in the 1950s. The municipal building at Gratiot and Meier Road went up in 1929 to replace the older Erin Township building near 11 Mile Road.

City government is council-manager, with voters electing six council members, a mayor, a clerk and a treasurer for staggered four-year terms. Roseville shares the 39th Judicial District with Fraser. If a buyer asks where legal and court business is handled, the district court is the starting point, and city hall at 29777 Gratiot Avenue handles bills and permits.

How did Roseville's population rise and fall?

The 1950s were a boom: the count jumped from 15,816 to 50,195 by 1960, then peaked at 60,529 in 1970. Since 1980 it has drifted between about 47,000 and 54,000.

What does the Census report about Roseville homes?

The 2020 to 2024 survey puts a typical Roseville owner-occupied home at $155,800, and 65.6 percent of homes are lived in by owners. Monthly ownership costs run $1,246 with a mortgage and $536 without.

  • Typical rent is $1,233 a month, close to the cost for owners who carry a mortgage.
  • The city has 21,226 households, 2.21 people each, with a typical income of $62,182.
  • Very few move in a year: 90.8 percent had the same address twelve months earlier.
  • Four-year degrees are held by 15.5 percent of adults over 25, and the poverty rate is 12.5 percent.

Use sold prices from your own street, rather than county averages, when you settle on an asking price.

How do roads and schools shape Roseville buying decisions?

Two freeways and two state routes make Roseville an easy commuter base. I-696, the Walter P. Reuther Freeway, crosses the middle from east to west, and I-94 runs along part of the border with St. Clair Shores. Gratiot Avenue (M-3) splits the city on its way from Detroit to Mount Clemens, while Groesbeck Highway (M-97) skirts the west side. Workers average 25.7 minutes getting to their jobs.

Neighbors are St. Clair Shores to the east, Eastpointe to the south, Warren to the west, and Fraser and Clinton Township to the north. The county seat of Mount Clemens is about 7 miles northeast.

Two districts teach children here. Roseville Community Schools operate seven elementary schools, two middle schools and a high school, and Fraser Public Schools runs two elementary schools inside the city limits. Conner Creek Academy East is a charter school in town. For shopping, Macomb Mall has anchored the area since 1964, west of Gratiot.

What does Roseville require of a rental house?

The city's Non-Owner Occupied Housing Ordinance governs rentals, and a unit that passes inspection earns a Certificate of Compliance. Once the owner submits an application and payment, the rental division calls to schedule the inspection.

  • Initial inspection and first reinspection: $150 for a single family house or duplex, $100 for apartments and condominiums.
  • Each additional unit at the same location, registered with the first: $50.
  • Lockout fee: $25.
  • Transfer of ownership: $25 for the first unit and $10 for each additional unit.

The city charges that ownership transfer fee on registered rentals, so ask the rental division who files the update and when. Give a buyer who plans to keep tenants your most recent Certificate of Compliance. You can reach the rental division at rentals@roseville-mi.gov, and it can tell you whether your address still needs a registration after the sale.

What do the buyer and seller file with Roseville assessing?

Roseville expects a Property Transfer Affidavit from the buyer within 45 days, and each late day costs $5 up to $200. At closing the buyer also signs the exemption form that saves 18 mills of school operating tax.

Sellers hand in a Request to Rescind Principal Residence at the Assessing Office, which clears the way for an exemption on the next home. From May onward the assessing staff inspect parcels that sold or have active building permits.

The assessor values property at half of its market value. Taxable value is allowed to rise each year only by the lesser of inflation and 5 percent, until a sale or physical change resets it. Owners who disagree must appeal by appointment or in writing before the March Board of Review closes.

What fees apply when a Roseville deed is filed in Macomb County?

Macomb charges the same $30 whether a deed runs two pages or twenty, with $3 more per extra instrument a document releases. Four dollars of the $30 is passed to a state survey fund.

Before a warranty deed or land contract is accepted, the treasurer stamps a tax certificate, priced at $5 for the first five legal descriptions. The recording office is on North Main Street in Mount Clemens.

On Macomb's schedule the state portion is the price times 0.0075 and the county portion is the price times 0.0011. Sellers are the ones who pay. Conveyances to a child or grandchild and foreclosure transfers are on the county's exemption list, and the deed has to say which exemption applies.

How do Roseville tax deadlines and penalties work?

Bills go out in July and December. Summer payments are due by August 31 and pick up a penalty of 1 percent per month from September 1; winter payments are due by February 28. Anything still open on March 1 is handed to the Macomb County Treasurer.

Homeowners who are 62 or older and earn under $40,000 can postpone the summer bill to February 28 for 1 percent monthly interest, if they file by September 15. Seniors can also get free help with state homestead credits.

A duplicate bill costs $2 a parcel. If you close soon after a due date, ask the title company to confirm payment so the buyer does not inherit a penalty.

Is there a Roseville fee when a rental changes hands?

Yes: $25 for the first unit and $10 for each added unit, according to the city's rental fee list.

What does filing a Roseville deed with Macomb County cost?

A flat $30, whatever the page count, with $4 going to the state survey fund. Warranty deeds also need a $5 tax certificate.

Which dates matter for Roseville property tax bills?

August 31 for summer, February 28 for winter, and March 1 when unpaid balances move to the Macomb County Treasurer.

Who owes the transfer tax on a Roseville sale?

The seller, at the 0.0075 state and 0.0011 county multipliers on Macomb's schedule.

How do I end my homestead exemption in Roseville?

File the city's Request to Rescind Principal Residence form with the Assessing Office, then claim the exemption on your next home.

How should a Saginaw owner approach a sale?

Saginaw homes sell at some of the lowest values in Michigan, so the way you sell can move your net more than the list price does. For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied value of $60,000, well under the state's larger metro areas.

Owners here usually pick from three routes:

  • An agent listing reaches the widest pool of buyers, with showings, inspections and a buyer's lender along the way.
  • A private sale keeps the commission in your pocket and leaves pricing and paperwork to you.
  • A cash sale as-is can fit vacant houses, tenant problems and inherited homes. Collect more than one offer and read the closing terms line by line.

City registration rules and county recording steps apply on every route, and they come up further down.

What is Saginaw like for someone selling a house?

Saginaw is the Saginaw County seat, set on the Saginaw River about 15 miles inland from Saginaw Bay, with roughly 17 square miles of land. Wikipedia places it in the middle of the state's largest watershed.

It started as a trading post and an Army fort after the 1819 Treaty of Saginaw, boomed on lumber in the 1800s and turned into a General Motors factory town in the 1900s. East Saginaw and Saginaw City joined in 1889 to form the present city.

Plant closures changed the numbers. The census counted 51,508 residents in 2010 and 44,202 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 42,863. Vacant houses have been part of that story: a 2013 federal blight program set aside $11.2 million for Saginaw, and the city began buying unwanted structures for demolition. If your house sits empty, deal with grass, boarding and utilities early, because a neglected house loses value faster than one that looks lived in.

What do Census numbers say about Saginaw housing?

Most Saginaw households own, but values and incomes sit well under the state picture. Treat the figures as background and look at recent sales on your own street for pricing.

Which neighborhoods, schools and roads do Saginaw buyers ask about?

Buyers sort Saginaw by neighborhood and by commute. Wikipedia's list includes Downtown, Old Town, Southwest Village, Heritage Square, Cathedral District, Brockway-Carmen Park, Sheridan Park, Northmoor and The Woods among its neighborhoods, along with the South East Side, Northeast Side and Northwest areas. Naming the neighborhood in a listing or an offer request tells a buyer what to expect on block condition.

Public schools come from Saginaw Public Schools, which Wikipedia lists with Saginaw United High School and the Saginaw Arts and Sciences Academy as the two public high schools. Michigan Lutheran Seminary is the city's only private high school. Delta College and Saginaw Valley State University are in nearby University Center, and a Delta College downtown site opened in fall 2019.

  • I-75 passes the east side through Buena Vista Charter Township.
  • I-675 loops through downtown and rejoins I-75.
  • M-13 runs from I-69 through downtown, and M-46 cuts across the Lower Peninsula through Saginaw.
  • M-47 serves the western suburbs and MBS International Airport.
  • STARS buses cover local routes, and Indian Trails handles intercity trips.

Big-box stores and Fashion Square Mall cluster along Bay Road and Tittabawassee Road in Saginaw Township, north of town.

How do Saginaw winters affect an older house?

Saginaw's climate is humid continental. NOAA normals quoted on Wikipedia list about 49 inches of snow and 32 inches of precipitation a year, a January mean low of 16.4 degrees Fahrenheit and a record low of minus 23.

Cold like that wears on roofs, gutters, foundations and heating equipment. A buyer's inspector in Michigan will look first at the roof, the furnace or boiler, basement moisture and plumbing in unheated spaces. Tell buyers about any past leak, frozen pipe or ice dam up front. A repair you explain reads better than one the buyer discovers later.

In a vacant house, keep the heat set low or drain the lines before the cold season. One burst pipe in an empty house can ruin a sellable property within a week.

What are the Saginaw rules for rentals and vacant houses?

The City Clerk keeps registries for rented and for unoccupied houses. Ordinance O-275, effective November 27, 2025, dropped the old rule that unpaid taxes or rubbish bills be cleared before a property could register, and the city now collects those amounts another way.

  • Rental owners register with the Clerk and file a current certificate of compliance where the code requires one.
  • Rental registrations expire each year on the fourth Friday of February, and a late renewal adds a 100 percent charge to the base fee.
  • A buyer who takes a rental or vacant house registers it within 60 days after title transfers.
  • An owner who lives in a one-dwelling house, alone or with immediate family, does not register it.
  • An owner who is actively advertising a registered rental for sale or rent does not also have to register it as unoccupied, with a copy of the advertisement as proof.

The unoccupied registry has a 12-month window after purchase for owners who are rehabilitating the house under permit. The Clerk's office, reachable at (989) 759-1480 extension 6, answers registration questions.

How do recording and transfer work for a Saginaw sale?

Deeds for Saginaw property go to the Saginaw County Register of Deeds. Its fee page lists $30 for each recorded document under MCL 600.2567, plus $3 for every extra instrument a document assigns or discharges. Copies run $1 a page and certification adds $5.

For tax certification the fee page says to contact the Saginaw County Treasurer. Ask both offices for the state and county transfer tax rates, and for who pays, so the figure appears on your settlement statement in advance.

Treasury's ownership FAQ says the buyer reports a change of ownership to the assessor on Form 2766 inside 45 days, citing MCL 211.27a(10). Settle property tax bills and city utility balances through the closing agent so nothing follows you to the next owner.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Saginaw house that needs major repairs?

Yes. Investors and cash buyers purchase repair-heavy Saginaw houses as-is. Expect the price to reflect the work, and gather permits, receipts and a list of known problems before you ask for offers.

Do I have to register my Saginaw rental before selling it?

A house occupied by someone other than you must be registered with the City Clerk, with renewal on the fourth Friday of February. The buyer registers within 60 days of taking title. Call the Clerk at (989) 759-1480 extension 6 about your case.

What does the county charge to record a Saginaw deed?

The Register of Deeds lists $30 per document. Transfer tax and tax certification are separate, so ask the Register and the County Treasurer for figures before closing.

Who files the ownership-change form after a Saginaw sale?

The buyer does. Michigan Treasury's guidance puts Form 2766, filed with the local assessor, within 45 days of the transfer. Mention it to your title company as a reminder.

Prices are low and the population fell from 51,508 in 2010 to an estimated 42,863 in July 2025, so a realistic price and patience help. Documented houses in steady neighborhoods still find buyers, and a cash sale avoids waiting on a buyer's loan.

What makes a Midland house sale different from other Michigan sales?

Midland certifies rentals through its own city program, posts its own tax calendar and records deeds at a flat county fee. Knowing those three items lets a seller schedule a sale without surprises.

Midland is estimated at 42,806 people for 2025, up 0.3% from 2020, across 34.37 square miles of land. That is a thin 1,238 residents per square mile. Owners live in 67.1% of the 18,535 households, with a median home value of $203,900 and rent of $1,048 at the median.

Median household income is $73,325, and 44.6% of adults finished a four-year degree. Poverty stands at 10.3%, commutes average 20 minutes, and 21.2% of residents are children while 20.4% are seniors. The city counts 2,205 veterans, 4.8% of residents were born abroad, and 90.8% of households have a broadband subscription.

Where is Midland and what drives its housing?

Midland is the Midland County seat, built where the Chippewa River joins the Tittabawassee. It lies roughly 24 miles northwest of Saginaw and 19 miles west of Bay City, with a small eastern piece in Bay County.

Dow Chemical began here in 1897 and remains the anchor employer, and its 2,600-acre Michigan Operations Industrial Park along Bay City Road supports about 6,000 employees and contractors. Tenants there include Corteva Agriscience, Hemlock Semiconductor and DuPont. Health care and education follow, with a 324-bed hospital in the MyMichigan system and Northwood University, while Midland Public Schools and Bullock Creek Public Schools cover K-12.

The city counts more than 35 neighborhoods, grouped by the city into eight general areas:

  • Downtown, including the Circle business district dating from 1938
  • North Side and Midland West, near the parks and river corridors
  • Country Club, known for large wooded lots
  • East End, where a Midtown revival started in 2018
  • Industrial Park and the small South area around the old Mapleton depot
  • West Main Street Historic District, set up in 1979

Utilities are worth a line in a listing. Brackish groundwater led the city to build a 65-mile pipeline from Lake Huron in 1948, and the city sells water to nearby townships under a long-running policy summed up as no annexation, no water. Consumers Energy supplies power and gas. City residents get weekly garbage and yard waste pickup and monthly collection of recyclables, large items and brush, while houses in unincorporated areas without municipal water rely on private wells and septic systems.

Inside the historic district, a commission signs off on construction, additions, repairs, moves and demolitions, so ask it before planning visible work. Drivers use US-10 along the north edge, M-20 toward Mount Pleasant and M-47 toward Saginaw and MBS International Airport. Midland has no regular scheduled bus; Dial-A-Ride operates within city limits.

Does the May 2020 flood matter to a Midland buyer?

It often does. Two upstream dams, Edenville and Sanford, failed on May 19, 2020, and about 10,000 Midland residents had to evacuate in what officials called a 500-year flood.

A house that took water, or sits close to either river, sells more smoothly with a paper trail: repair invoices, permits, insurance claims and remediation records. A repaired basement with documents is easier to price than one nobody can account for.

Everyday weather leaves marks too. Annual precipitation is 33.41 inches and snowfall 31.4 inches, with January highs near 29 degrees, so roofs, gutters and furnaces get a real test each winter.

What does Midland require of a house that has been a rental?

Midland inspects and certifies each home, duplex, rooming house, short-term rental and apartment that its owner does not occupy, and the unit may not be rented until certified. That includes houses where no rent is collected and houses occupied by relatives.

A homeowner may keep up to two boarders in a single-family house without an inspection; a third renter triggers one. Four unrelated tenants is the cap for any rental unit. Fees changed on July 1, 2025 to:

  • Rooming house: $105
  • Other rental units: $79 for the first unit and $36 for each extra unit
  • First reinspection per unit: free, with later ones billed at the certification rate
  • Late certification: $36 per unit, with the full certification fee repeated at 30 and at 60 days of delay

The Rental Program takes calls at (989) 837-3383, option 1, or email at rentalprogram@midland-mi.org. Any plan to rent the house for a few months before selling it needs the certificate first.

Which Midland tax dates should a seller watch?

Midland mails summer bills on July 1 and winter bills on December 1, and December 31 is Tax Day, the date that fixes the next year's value and classification. The city posts the full calendar and notes that the dates stay close to constant.

Midland tax calendar

March 1Unpaid real property taxes pass to the Midland County Treasurer
2nd Monday in MarchBoard of Review hears value and classification appeals

Source: City of Midland, Important Tax Related Dates. A buyer who lives in the house by June 1 qualifies for the summer bill's exemption, and moving in by November 1 covers the winter bill. MCL 211.27a resets taxable value after a sale, so the buyer's first bill will likely differ from yours.

What happens at the Midland County Register of Deeds?

Recording costs $30 for any document, however many pages it has. The office sits at 220 W Ellsworth Street and keeps weekday hours of 8 to 5.

  • A warranty deed or land contract needs a $5 certificate proving taxes are current.
  • Transfer tax runs $4.30 per $500 of the sale amount, state and county combined.
  • Copies are $1 a page and a certified copy adds $5.
  • Qualified submitters can e-record, but court orders and death certificates carry a raised seal and go in on paper.
  • The office will not draft a deed or advise on one.

Under MCL 207.526 a deed from parent to child, or grandparent to grandchild, owes no state transfer tax.

Which sale route suits a Midland house?

Match the route to your timeline and the house's condition. A listing works for a sound house with time on the calendar, a private sale for an owner who will do the legwork, and a cash purchase for a house with tenants, flood repairs or a rental certificate still pending.

Give us the Midland address and a rundown of the repairs, and we will quote a price for the house as it stands. Set that figure next to what a listing would net after repairs and fees.

Frequently asked questions

May I rent my Midland house out while it is for sale?

Only after the city inspects and certifies it. The certification fee is $79 for the first unit, and each late month adds charges.

By what date does a Midland buyer need to claim the principal residence exemption?

The buyer must own and occupy the house by June 1 for the summer bill or November 1 for the winter bill, and files the affidavit with the city.

Who collects Midland taxes that go unpaid?

The Midland County Treasurer. Real property taxes still unpaid on March 1 are turned over to the county.

What is the recording charge for a Midland deed?

$30 per document covers recording. A warranty deed adds a $5 certificate, and transfer tax is billed on the sale price.

Should I mention the 2020 dam failures when I sell a Midland house?

Yes when the property flooded or lies near the Chippewa or Tittabawassee. Keep repair and insurance records handy for questions from buyers and lenders.

What does a seller in Lincoln Park have to do that sellers in most Michigan cities do not?

A Lincoln Park seller needs a Certificate of Approval from the city's Building Department before the house can be transferred. The city's ordinance on inspection of residential dwellings prior to sale makes it unlawful to transfer a dwelling, or to act as a broker for the transfer, without a current certificate.

The rule shapes the timeline of every sale in the city, however you find your buyer. The rest of this page explains how the certificate works, then covers the city, its housing figures and the tax and recording steps that follow.

How does the Lincoln Park Certificate of Approval work?

The ordinance (Chapter 1488 of the city's codified ordinances) requires anyone about to transfer a dwelling to register with the Building Department so an inspection can be scheduled. The fee is set by City Council resolution, so ask the department for the current amount.

The main points of the chapter:

  • A Certificate of Approval is valid for one sale or transfer, and a new inspection is required each time the dwelling is sold again.
  • A dwelling includes the house and accessory uses such as garages, sheds, pools, gazebos and playhouses.
  • A buyer may take responsibility for correcting violations by signing a notarized affidavit filed with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited.
  • Failing to obtain the certificate is a municipal civil infraction with a $500 fine.

Inspectors may enter the premises during normal business hours to inspect, and owners, agents and occupants must give access to every part of the property they control. The enforcing official can also order immediate action to remove a hazard. Clear access to the garage, sheds and any pool or gazebo before the inspection date, because accessory structures are part of what the ordinance covers.

A transfer means a sale, a land contract or the exercise of an option to purchase. Gifts, devises and lien foreclosures are outside the definition. Rentals follow a separate track, covered below.

How are the certificates for owner-occupied and rental houses different?

Lincoln Park uses different certificates for different situations, and sellers sometimes confuse them. The table summarizes the three named in the ordinance.

Certificates in Lincoln Park Chapter 1488, City of Lincoln Park codified ordinances
CertificateApplies toHow long it lasts
Certificate of ApprovalResidential dwelling being sold or transferredOne sale or transfer
Certificate of ComplianceRental dwellings and rental unitsThree years, unless the property is sold first
Certificate of OccupancyApproved use or occupancy under the zoning ordinancesIssued by the Building Department

A rental that holds a current Certificate of Compliance is not treated as a dwelling for the Certificate of Approval rule, but a new inspection and a new Certificate of Compliance are required before a rental is sold or transferred. If you own a rental, schedule that inspection before you sign a contract.

What is Lincoln Park like, and who lives there?

Lincoln Park is a Downriver suburb of Detroit in Wayne County, about 11 miles southwest of downtown. With only 5.84 square miles of land and 6,896 people per square mile in 2020, it ranked second in Michigan for density, behind Hamtramck. By the July 2025 estimate the city has 38,529 residents, down 4.3 percent from the 2020 base.

Its neighbors are Detroit, Allen Park, Melvindale, Ecorse, Wyandotte and Southgate. The north and south branches of the Ecorse River run through town and join before leaving it. Council Point Park marks the 1763 meeting where Pontiac urged tribal leaders to join him against Fort Detroit.

The city was laid out in 1906 as part of Ecorse Township, became a village in 1921 and a city in 1925. It grew as a bedroom community for workers at the River Rouge Plant and other auto and steel works, and two shopping centers opened in 1955 and 1956. Lincoln Park Public Schools serves residents through Lincoln Park High School, Lincoln Park Middle School and seven elementary schools.

What do the Census figures say about Lincoln Park homes?

The 2020 to 2024 figures describe a compact, owner-heavy city with a modest median value.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $131,000
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 68.8%, with 14,767 households
  • Median gross rent: $1,023
  • Median monthly owner costs: $1,169 with a mortgage, $530 without
  • Same house one year ago: 91.3%

  • Residents under 18: 25.5%, also the highest of the four

Those figures, together with a bachelor's degree rate of 11.5 percent and a poverty rate of 21.5 percent, show a price level where a five-figure repair matters a great deal to a net result. Price the house with the inspection list in hand, since a buyer will do the same.

When are Lincoln Park property taxes due?

The city treasurer collects only current-year taxes. Summer bills are mailed by the end of June and fall due August 20, with later installment dates for owners who pay in parts, and a 1 percent penalty applies on the 20th of each month to unpaid summer taxes. Winter bills are mailed around the end of November and are due in mid-February, with a 1 percent monthly penalty after that.

All unpaid taxes transfer to the Wayne County Treasurer on March 1. The processor adds 2.95 percent to online payments, and a duplicate bill costs $10 unless you print the record from the city site. Title companies, agents and landlords are told this in a notice on the city's tax page.

Business personal property is taxed through the same office. Anyone operating on December 31 owes the following year's entire billing cycle, under state law.

How are a Lincoln Park deed and transfer tax handled?

Lincoln Park deeds are recorded by the Wayne County Register of Deeds. The Wayne County Treasurer must certify taxes on a deed first in most cases, and visits are by appointment. The fee schedule that began January 1, 2026 sets a deed at $26, with a $4 survey fee where it applies.

The state tax comes to $3.75 per $500 of price, with a separate county tax. State law exempts some conveyances, for example a deed given in foreclosure and a land contract that has not yet passed title, so ask the title company whether yours qualifies.

Afterward, the buyer sends the assessor a transfer affidavit within 45 days, and your own homestead exemption should be cancelled within 90 days of your move.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Lincoln Park?

Yes. Lincoln Park requires a Certificate of Approval from the Building Department before a dwelling is transferred, and a new one for every sale. Register with the department so it can schedule the inspection, and ask what the council-set fee is.

What is the fine for selling without a Certificate of Approval?

The ordinance sets the fine for failing to obtain a Certificate of Approval at $500, as a municipal civil infraction. It also states that other statutory and common-law rights and actions are not limited by that penalty, so a buyer or the city may have further remedies.

Can a buyer take over the violations in Lincoln Park?

Yes, by signing a notarized affidavit that states the buyer's intent to correct them and filing it with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited, so a buyer needs a realistic repair budget and schedule.

What does the Census say a Lincoln Park house is worth?

Lincoln Park's median owner-occupied home value is $131,000 for 2020 to 2024, and median gross rent is $1,023.

When do unpaid Lincoln Park taxes go to the county?

Come March 1, everything unpaid belongs to the county treasurer, and the city no longer takes those payments.

What should a Muskegon seller expect from the city and county?

Muskegon sellers deal with a city that registers and inspects every rental, a lake-effect climate that is hard on roofs, and a county office that records deeds for a flat fee. A house that was ever a rental carries the most paperwork.

Census estimates put the city at 37,224 people for 2025, level with its 2020 base. Of 13,996 households, 53.1% own their home. Owned homes are valued at $142,300 at the median, rent is $996, and owners with a mortgage pay a median of $1,064 a month. At those prices, a repair bill of a few thousand dollars takes a big bite out of a sale.

Median household income is $44,735, and 24.9% of residents live below the poverty line. Children make up 22.4% of the population and seniors 14.8%, only 15.5% of adults hold a four-year degree, and commutes average 20.6 minutes. Roughly 81% of residents stayed in the same house over the past year.

Where is Muskegon, and what shapes its housing?

Muskegon is the Muskegon County seat, a harbor city on the south shore of Muskegon Lake with Lake Michigan just beyond. Its 18.20 square miles include 4.05 of water, or 22.3%.

The Muskegon River enters the lake at the northeast end. Neighbors include North Muskegon, Muskegon Township, Fruitport Township, Muskegon Heights, Roosevelt Park and Norton Shores, and Grand Rapids lies 42 miles to the southeast. Lumber drew settlers beginning in 1837, which earned the city nicknames such as Lumber Queen of the World, and Bluffton, once its own lumber village, was annexed in 1889.

  • Downtown: about two miles of lakefront with hotels, a 25,000-square-foot convention center completed in 2021 and the Trinity Health Arena.
  • Schools: Muskegon Public Schools dates to 1860, and Muskegon Community College and Baker College are in the area.
  • Travel: I-96, US 31, M-46 and M-120 serve the city, MATS runs buses and trolleys, and the Lake Express car ferry crosses to Milwaukee.
  • Flights: Muskegon County Airport has nonstop service to Chicago O'Hare.

The waterfront is a draw. The Saturday farmers market in summer welcomes more than 10,000 visitors, boutique shops fill Western Avenue, and trolley stops include the USS Silversides and Muskegon State Park. In May 2022 local groups announced that cleanup work on Muskegon Lake was finished, which began the EPA's review of removing the lake from its list of Areas of Concern. The city runs under a seven-member commission and a hired city manager.

Snow is the main wear factor. A year brings 87.2 inches, with January alone at 29.1 inches, and 48 days with measurable snow, mostly lake-effect. Roofs, gutters and furnaces take that punishment, and an inspector on the buyer's side will start there.

Which Muskegon rental rules follow a house into a sale?

Every rental in the city must be registered and inspected, and the certificate stays with the owner who earned it. Anyone buying with a rental plan starts fresh, with a new certificate and a new inspection.

A clean first inspection earns a 6-year certificate, while violations put the property on a 3-year cycle. Because the city works under the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, rentals need carbon monoxide readers, and a licensed contractor must certify the furnace and water heater at 0 ppm in the breathable area. An owner who lives more than 30 miles off must name a responsible party within 30 miles.

Does a Muskegon short-term rental license go with the house?

Usually not. Licenses issued after the ordinance was adopted cannot be transferred, so the registration stays with the owner who obtained it.

One exception exists for properties with an active short-term rental status before March 2024. They may make a one-time status transfer in any zone using a signed formal document, and the new owner still completes registration and inspections. The overlay district has 11 zones with caps ranging from 13 in Zone 11 to 95 in Zone 9, and Zone 1, Beachwood and Bluffton, is full with a waitlist. Properties inside the downtown authority, the Lakeside Business Improvement District and the Lakeside Corridor Improvement Authority fall outside the caps.

A single-family short-term rental pays $500 a year, with each added unit adding another $500. Any buyer whose offer rests on vacation-rental income should read the overlay rules before signing.

What are the Muskegon tax deadlines at closing?

The city bills in two rounds. Summer bills issue July 1 and are due September 14, and winter bills issue December 1 and are due February 14.

Summer taxes left unpaid collect 1% interest monthly once past due and a 3% penalty if still open on February 14, while winter taxes take a 3% penalty after their due date. Whatever the city has not collected by February 28 becomes delinquent on March 1 and the County Treasurer collects it. Your title company will prorate the current bill at the closing table.

The buyer's taxable value is reset the year after the sale (MCL 211.27a), which can lift the next bill well above yours. If you claimed the principal residence exemption, rescind it within 90 days of moving out or face $5 a day, up to $200 (MCL 211.7cc).

What does recording cost at the Muskegon County Register of Deeds?

One flat charge applies: $30 per deed, mortgage or other instrument, however many pages.

  • Warranty deeds, land contracts and assignments with a warranty clause first need a $5 certificate from the County Treasurer's Office.
  • Real estate record copies run $1 a page, plus $5 per certification.
  • Combined transfer tax is $4.30 per $500 of price, so a $150,000 sale pays $1,290.
  • A free Fraud Guard alert emails you whenever your name appears on a recorded document.

Gifts between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild are exempt from state transfer tax (MCL 207.526).

The choices are a listing, a sale by owner or a cash purchase. Weigh repair costs, carrying costs and timing against price, because a lower-priced house can lose a bigger share of its value to fixes.

Before you talk to buyers, gather:

  • The rental certificate and latest furnace and water heater inspection, if the house was rented
  • The latest summer and winter tax bills, so the closing agent can settle what is owed
  • Records of roof, gutter and basement work after a lake-effect winter
  • Your deed or land contract paperwork

For a cash price, send us the Muskegon address and the house's condition. We buy as-is, so a failed rental inspection or a winter-damaged roof need not be fixed first.

No. Rental certificates do not transfer to new owners, so a buyer opens a new certificate, passes an inspection and pays the registration fee. Mention that early if your buyer plans to rent the house out.

How long does a Muskegon rental certificate last?

Six years after a clean first inspection and three years when violations are found. The yearly registration fee keeps it in good standing between inspections.

When do unpaid Muskegon taxes go to the county?

March 1. The city passes along anything uncollected by February 28, and the County Treasurer takes over from there.

$1,290, made up of $1,125 state tax and $165 county tax.

What does a Muskegon short-term rental registration cost?

$500 a year for a single-family unit, rising to $1,000 for a duplex and $2,500 for a quinplex. Reinspections start at $100 and climb in $100 steps.

Why does Holland's county line matter to a seller?

Holland straddles a county line, and that touches nearly every step. Thirty-second Street divides the city between Ottawa County on the north and Allegan County on the south, so the deed, the treasurer and the school district can all depend on which side your house stands. Whether the house is listed, sold privately or bought for cash, first confirm which county holds your parcel.

The city sits beside Lake Macatawa, about 5 miles east of Lake Michigan, and its 17.45 square miles split into 9.08 on the Ottawa side and 8.13 on the Allegan side. It is the biggest city in each county. Estimates for mid-2025 put the population at 35,372, up 2.9 percent from the 2020 base, the only one of the four cities in this batch that grew.

What is the Holland housing market built on?

Dutch Calvinist settlers under Albertus van Raalte arrived in 1847, and Holland received its city charter in 1867. A fire on October 8 to 10, 1871 burned most of downtown, which is why older homes gather in the Historic District and around it. Neighborhoods people mention include Holland Heights, Westside, Washington Square, Hope, Maplewood, South End and Downtown.

Jobs come from manufacturing, tourism, agriculture and higher education. Employers listed for the area include Herman Miller, Haworth, Adient, Magna and Kraft Heinz, with Hope College and a Grand Valley State University campus in town. The Tulip Time festival each May brings visitors who book local homes, so the short-term rental rules below include a festival category.

Where do Holland prices and ownership rates stand?

Holland leads Hamtramck, Jackson and Kalamazoo on home value. Survey estimates for 2020 through 2024:

  • Typical owner-occupied home: $252,200.
  • Homeownership: 67.8 percent of 12,977 households.
  • Typical rent: $1,193.
  • Persons per household: 2.34, and 23.6 percent of residents are Hispanic or Latino.
  • Average trip to work: 16.8 minutes.

Short commutes and a mix of furniture and automotive employers support demand, yet a house needing a roof, furnace or foundation work still sells below the typical price. A cash buyer pricing a repair-heavy house starts from the repaired value and subtracts the work.

Which offices and schools serve my Holland house?

Nearly all of the Ottawa County side lies inside Holland Public Schools. On the Allegan side, Holland Public Schools covers most of the area and Hamilton Community Schools the remainder. The city's own millage table reflects this with a separate Hamilton line.

Each deed goes to the register of deeds for its own county. Ottawa County records at its office on Fillmore Street in West Olive and offers a web portal for one-off e-recording, while Allegan County's register handles the southern side. Overdue taxes are a county matter, handled by the Ottawa or Allegan treasurer; the current bill itself comes from the city treasurer.

What does a Holland tax bill include, and what is the deadline?

The city dates the summer bill July 1 and sets the payment deadline in mid-August; the 2026 summer bill was due August 17. The winter bill follows on December 1. The city adds a 1 percent administration fee to both bills. Qualifying seniors and disabled homestead owners may ask to defer the summer payment; a 2026 deferral moved the due date to February 16, 2027.

Source: City of Holland tax estimator page. The 18-mill gap between the two columns is the school operating tax that a homeowner's exemption removes, so an investor who will not occupy the home pays the higher rate.

Can a buyer or tenant use my Holland house as a rental?

Chapter 14 of Holland's ordinance code governs rentals, which matters if tenants live in the house you are selling. Each unit must be registered, and the annual fee carries a December 10 deadline. An unregistered rental or unreported change draws a $200 late fee, and an unpaid annual fee is a misdemeanor. Inspections come every 3 or 6 years, the guide for monthly or annual leases lists a 3-year cycle, and a passing unit earns a Certificate of Compliance.

Short-term stays follow a separate track, and the city sorts them into three types:

  • Owner-occupied: your own primary residence, permitted in every zone.
  • Investor-owned: a home the owner does not live in. Permitted in mixed-use, industrial and similar districts; in residential districts, only within a cap of 25 properties and a 500-foot spacing rule. Ask the city whether any slots remain.
  • Tulip Time: a home offered no more than 10 days during the May festival, with no inspection or certificate required.

A buyer planning an investor-owned short-term rental in a residential zone should confirm capacity with the city first.

How is transfer tax figured on a Holland sale?

Sellers pay it. Michigan's state rate is $3.75 per $500 of price (MCL 207.525), and a county with under 2,000,000 residents adds 55 cents per $500 (MCL 207.504). A $250,000 price equals 500 units at $4.30, which is $2,150, payable to the county treasurer inside 15 days after the deed is delivered.

MCL 207.526 exempts gifts to a child or grandchild, court-ordered transfers with no set price, and deeds from foreclosed government-backed loans. If your lot touches 32nd Street, ask the register in each county how the parcel is recorded.

Which Holland tax exemptions end or start when the house sells?

Your principal residence exemption changes at closing. State law (MCL 211.7cc) has the owner file a rescission no later than 90 days after the house stops serving as a principal residence. A newcomer who moves in files an affidavit; the deadline is June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy. Holland's assessing office handles both forms.

Holland's tax page names other relief as well: a home repair exemption under Public Act 25 of 1978 that holds assessed value steady up to the sale, a poverty exemption (MCL 211.7u), and relief for disabled veterans. If you used any of them, tell the buyer, because the first bill after closing may look different.

How do the lake and climate affect a Holland house?

Lake Michigan tempers Holland's climate, which is classed as humid continental. January daily highs average 31.8 degrees with lows near 19.9, and an all-time low of minus 24 shows that a furnace failure in the winter can freeze pipes. Summer highs average 81.7 degrees in July. Homes near Lake Macatawa and the Macatawa River sit at about 610 feet of elevation, so expect your buyer's inspector to check basements for moisture, and fix gutters or grading before showings.

Frequently asked questions

In which county is my Holland deed recorded?

The one that holds your parcel. Holland spans Ottawa County (north) and Allegan County (south) with 32nd Street as the boundary, and each keeps its own register of deeds.

When is the City of Holland summer tax due?

Mid-August. The 2026 summer bill was dated July 1 and fell due August 17. A 1 percent administration fee is added to the summer and winter bills.

What happens to my Holland rental registration when I sell?

Registration and certification belong to the rental operation, and the city wants ownership changes reported. A missed report costs a $200 late fee, so tell the city about the sale.

Can my buyer operate a short-term rental in Holland?

Owner-occupied ones are allowed in every zone. Investor-owned ones in residential districts are limited to 25 properties with 500 feet of spacing, so check capacity first.

What is the transfer tax on a $200,000 Holland sale?

$1,720: 400 units of $500 at $3.75 for the state and $0.55 for the county. Family transfers to a child or grandchild are exempt.

What should an Eastpointe homeowner know before selling?

Eastpointe is a small, dense Macomb County city of 5.16 square miles, and most of what sellers deal with is rental registration, tax billing and school boundaries rather than a pre-sale inspection. Owners live in about seven of every ten homes, so many buyers are families looking for a first or second home.

The community was first settled by Irish and German immigrants in the 1830s. A post office opened in October 1897 under the name Half-way, because the spot sat near the halfway point of the stage run between downtown Detroit and the county seat at Mount Clemens. It became the village of Halfway in 1924 and the city of East Detroit in 1929. Voters approved the name Eastpointe in a 1992 referendum, partly to separate the city's identity from Detroit and to echo the nearby Grosse Pointes.

Downtown Detroit is ten miles southwest of Eastpointe. Warren lies to the west, Roseville to the north and St. Clair Shores to the east, and 8 Mile Road forms the southern edge beside Detroit and Harper Woods.

How does Eastpointe housing look in the Census figures?

The city peaked at 45,920 residents in 1970, slipped to 32,442 by 2010 and has hovered near 34,000 since. The rows below give the Census Bureau's latest local figures.

A typical rent of $1,325 is close to what Dearborn renters pay, even though owned homes here are worth far less. Rents that high against modest home values make rented houses common, so the city's rental registration rules come up in many sales.

Do Eastpointe rental and vacant property rules affect a sale?

They can. The Building Department manages registration and inspection of every non-owner-occupied residential property, and tenants cannot occupy a rental until the city certifies it. If your house is rented, the buyer inherits that regime.

  • Rentals must be registered and inspected every two years from the application date.
  • If a property is certified at the time of sale, the certificate may transfer to the new owner when that owner registers within 14 days of purchase.
  • Owners and property managers complete a one-time registration separate from the property registration.
  • An owner who lives 50 miles or more from city hall must name a local agent.
  • A furnace or boiler must pass an inspection by a qualified contractor.

Vacant buildings have their own rule: register inside 45 days of the vacancy, renew each year until the property is occupied again, and obtain a certificate of compliance for re-occupancy. Call the Building Department at 586-445-3661 for rentals (extension 2269) or vacant properties (extension 2214).
